copy.privacy.title: Privacy policy
copy.privacy.intro: This policy explains, in plain English, what the lanckrietchess Training Hub (the “hub”) does with your data. The short version: the hub is built to keep your training on your own device, and it only sends something to a server when a feature needs it or when you choose to share it.
copy.privacy.s1.title: At a glance
copy.privacy.s1.text:
- **No ads and no tracking.** The hub has no advertising, no analytics service and no tracking cookies, and it never sells your data.
- **Your training stays on your device.** Progress, streaks, games, mistakes and repertoires live in your own browser unless you switch on a feature that shares part of it.
- **Sharing is your choice.** The leaderboards, friends, the community ELO board and anonymous training stats are opt-in, and you can switch them off again.
- **What you type is used for what you asked.** A support question or an application goes to {coach} and nowhere else.
- **You stay in control.** You can reset your progress, leave the boards, disconnect your chess accounts and ask for your data to be deleted.
copy.privacy.s2.title: Who is responsible
copy.privacy.s2.text:
The controller of your data is Kyenzo Lanckriet (lanckrietchess), based in Middelkerke, Belgium. The hub is a progressive web app: you open it in your browser, install it on your phone, or open it inside the Skool classroom.

Because the controller is based in Belgium, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Belgian data protection law apply. You can reach {coach} through the contact options at the bottom of this page.
copy.privacy.s3.title: What stays on your device
copy.privacy.s3.text:
The hub stores the following in your browser’s local storage, on your own device. None of it is sent anywhere unless a section below says so:
- Your profile: the name or username you choose, your rating, main leak, goal, working points and check-ins, your struggles and your repertoire choices.
- Your progress: accuracy, streaks, finished drills, badges, mistakes saved for spaced repetition, your Puzzle ELO and your credits.
- Your games and positions: reviewed games, the Game Vault, brilliant moves, your own repertoires and your last Trim session.
- Your membership: the member key you entered and a random device ID that identifies this browser to the hub.
- Your settings, your friends list and the answers you gave in the Upgrades chat.

The hub does not use cookies for this. The profile token and the coach briefing in your profile are created on your device; if you copy them into another service, that service receives what they contain. Stockfish, the chess engine, also runs on your device and sends nothing anywhere.

Reset my progress in your profile removes your progress. Clearing the site data in your browser removes everything, and that cannot be undone.
copy.privacy.s4.title: What is sent to the hub’s server
copy.privacy.s4.text:
The hub can connect to a server run for lanckrietchess (the “Arena server”, hosted on Cloudflare with a database). It is only used when {coach} has switched it on, and only for the features below:
- **Leaderboards and tournament.** If you join, your chosen username, your rating bracket, your puzzle results and your scores are stored and shown to other players. Without a username you are not shown.
- **Puzzle ELO and Trim boards.** Your username, bracket, Puzzle ELO and peak, your rated puzzle results, and counts of games reviewed and blunders solved.
- **Community ELO board.** If you connect Chess.com or Lichess, the server checks a one-time code in your profile and reads your public username, avatar and ratings from that site, then shows them on the board.
- **Friends.** Your friend card (name, rating, weekly progress, top working point, tournament score and your latest blunder) when you share your friend code. Your MSPC system (band and top five working points) is added by default, so friends who have your code can see it. Switch that off at the very bottom of your profile settings or in Account > MSPC System. With the server on, friends who have your code can fetch your latest card.
- **Peer puzzles.** When you review a game in Trim, your blunders and mistakes can be staged as puzzles: the position, the move you played, the better move, the opening, your name and rating. Positions from the hub’s own repertoire courses go to {coach} for review, including the moves of that game. Other positions can be offered to other players as free peer puzzles.
- **Anonymous training stats.** Only if you agree: which drills you miss, where your games leak, what you ask the coach (with emails, links and phone numbers removed) and Trim results. They are stored under a random ID that is not linked to your name, member key or leaderboard entry. Reviewed games and positions can be included without names.
- **Membership.** When you enter a member key, the server checks it and ties it to one device, using your random device ID.
copy.privacy.s5.title: The AI coach
copy.privacy.s5.text:
The Pro coach, a paid-member feature, answers through an AI model. The same goes for the Growth Path assistants, but only if {coach} has switched them on. When you type a question, the hub sends your message and the recent conversation, the position on the board and the moves of the game you are looking at, Stockfish’s lines, the review of the move you are on, and a short profile (name or username, rating, main leak, goal, working points, struggles and repertoire) to the Arena server. The server forwards this to the AI provider, Anthropic (Claude), and your member key is sent so the server can confirm your membership.

The free coach does not use AI: its question buttons are answered on your device.

Please do not type anything into the coach that you would not want processed by an AI provider, such as contact details or health information. Anthropic processes the request to produce an answer, under its own terms and privacy policy.
copy.privacy.s6.title: Messages, questions and applications
copy.privacy.s6.text:
Some features send what you type to {coach}, or to tools he uses to receive and organise requests:
- **Support questions and timeline answers.** Your name, your email or Instagram handle, your message or answer, your rating, the answers you gave in the Upgrades chat and your membership level.
- **Mentorship application.** Your name, contact, a one-line reason, your rating and where it comes from, your Chess.com and Lichess usernames, your goal, your Trim leak and how often it came back, your working points and a short application note. It is only sent after you tick the consent box, and you see what will be sent first.
- **Links to Instagram, Skool or an application form** open in a new tab. What happens there is covered by that service’s own privacy policy.

These messages may pass through automation tools such as Make, Zapier or ManyChat. They are used only to answer you, to handle your application and to keep a record of it.
copy.privacy.s7.title: Other services you connect to
copy.privacy.s7.text:
Opening the hub makes your browser contact a few services. They can see your IP address and basic technical data such as your browser, device and the time of the request:
- **Vercel** hosts the hub.
- **GitHub** serves the course data file and its version information.
- **Content delivery networks** (cdnjs, jsDelivr, Google Fonts, Tailwind CSS and Font Awesome) deliver code, fonts and icons.
- **Lichess** supplies rated puzzles, and **Chess.com** and Lichess supply public profile data when you connect or follow an account. The hub never asks for a password for either.
- **Skool** hosts the community, the classroom and the memberships. It has its own privacy policy.

We do not control the logs of these services. The hub never asks for or stores payment card details: memberships are paid on Skool.
copy.privacy.s8.title: Legal basis and how long data is kept
copy.privacy.s8.text:
Under the GDPR we process data on these grounds:
- **Consent** (Article 6(1)(a)) for the leaderboards, friends and community ELO features, anonymous training stats, support questions, applications and the questions you choose to send to the AI coach. You can withdraw consent at any time; this does not affect what happened before.
- **Performance of a contract** (Article 6(1)(b)) for member keys: checking your key and tying it to your device so you get the membership you have.
- **Legitimate interest** (Article 6(1)(f)) for keeping the hub secure and fair, for example limiting requests, checking that scores are plausible and hiding abusive usernames.

How long we keep it:
- Data on your device stays until you erase it.
- Leaderboard, tournament, friend and rating-board data on the server stays while you take part. It is deleted when you leave the board or switch the feature off, or when you ask.
- Anonymous training stats are deleted from the server when you switch sharing off.
- Support questions and applications are kept for as long as needed to answer them and to keep a record of your application. They are deleted on request.
- The services in the previous section follow their own retention periods.
copy.privacy.s9.title: Your choices in the app
copy.privacy.s9.text:
Where to find the controls:
- **Profile, community leaderboard.** Join or leave the boards. Leaving removes you from the server board.
- **Profile, anonymous training stats.** Switch it off and what was shared is deleted.
- **Profile, chess accounts.** Connect or disconnect Chess.com and Lichess. Disconnecting removes you from the community ELO board.
- **Profile, membership.** Remove your member key from this device.
- **Profile, reset my progress,** and the delete options in your Game Vault and My repertoire.
- **Friends.** Remove any friend. Your own friend code only contains what you see on your card. Your MSPC system and working points are included by default; switch that off at the very bottom of your profile settings.
- **Settings.** Achievement pop-ups and spaced repetition can be switched off in your profile.
- **Your browser.** Clearing the site data removes everything the hub stores on your device.
copy.privacy.s10.title: Your rights
copy.privacy.s10.text:
You have the right to:
- ask for access to the data we hold about you,
- have inaccurate data corrected,
- have your data erased,
- restrict or object to the processing,
- receive your data in a portable form,
- withdraw your consent at any time,
- not be subject to a decision based only on automated processing. The hub’s scores, ratings and recommendations only steer your training and never decide anything legal about you.

To use a right, contact {coach} through the options at the bottom of this page. To find your entries on the server, give your username, and your friend code if you have one. If we cannot identify you from the request, we may ask for proof that the data is yours. We answer within one month.

You can also lodge a complaint with the Belgian Data Protection Authority (Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit / Autorité de protection des données, www.dataprotectionauthority.be) or with the supervisory authority in your own EU country.
copy.privacy.s11.title: Security and international transfers
copy.privacy.s11.text:
Connections to the hub and its servers use HTTPS. Member keys are published only as one-way hashes, and a key is tied to a single device. The key for the AI provider is kept on the server, never in the app. No system is perfectly secure, and anything stored in your browser can be read by someone with access to your device, so please use a screen lock.

Some of the services above operate from outside the European Economic Area, for example in the United States. Where that happens they rely on safeguards such as the EU–US Data Privacy Framework or Standard Contractual Clauses.
copy.privacy.s12.title: Children and changes
copy.privacy.s12.text:
The hub is not meant for children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect data from them. If you are below the age of digital consent in your country (13 in Belgium, up to 16 elsewhere in the EU), ask a parent or guardian before you share anything beyond your own device, such as joining a leaderboard or sending a message.

We may update this policy when the hub changes, for example when a feature that uses data is added. The date at the top shows the last update, and a change that affects your choices will be made visible in the hub.
copy.privacy.contact: Questions about your data, or a request to see, correct or delete it? Message {coach} directly. He answers himself. Please mention your username in the hub so he can find your entries.

# The MSPC System [free] | mspc
## M, Move: read their last move | M, threat, check, hanging
- What did their move change? | Every move attacks, defends or prepares something. Name it before you choose your own move.
- The threat scan | Before every move: which checks, captures and attacks does your opponent have now?
## S, Specifics: what this position is about | S, loose, hanging, structure, king, plan
- Loose pieces drop off | An undefended piece is a target. Count the defenders of every piece before you move.
- What the structure asks for | The pawn structure tells you where to play: the break, the outpost, the weak square.
## P, Priorities: checks, captures, attacks | P, forcing, check, capture, fork, pin, skewer, mate
- Checks, captures and attacks for both sides | List your forcing moves, then theirs. Forcing moves first, quiet moves after.
- Take the initiative | A forcing move that gains time beats a quiet move that only reacts.
## C, Calculation: to the end | C, calculation, sacrifice, mate
- Calculate to the end | Follow every forcing line until the position is quiet, including their best reply.
- The calculation cutoff | Do not stop halfway out of fear or hope: the reply you skipped is the one that beats you.

# Endgame Suite [vault] | endgame
## Laws that decide endgames [free] | endgame, basics | #endgame
- The laws that decide endgames (level 1) | Level 1. Before technique, know when a game is already over: stalemate, dead position, repetition, the 50-move rule, flag-fall and the free choice of promotion piece.
## Winconditions: the two ways endgames end [free] | endgame, basics | #endgame
- Winconditions: the two ways endgames end (level 1) | Level 1. Every endgame ends with exactly one of two mechanisms: a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition. Everything else is a lever that helps you create, execute or deny one.
- The Endgame Scan and the Conversion Ladder (level 2) | Level 2. A five-step scan tells you what to do whenever the position changes character, and a four-rung ladder shows how every won endgame is converted.
- Wincondition denial: the defender's mirror (level 3) | Level 3. The defender has seven ways to deny a Wincondition: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual check and a counter-Wincondition.
- Anchor positions and zones (level 4) | Level 4. Theory is a map of targets: steer toward winning anchors and away from drawn ones, and know the zones where the defending king must stand.
- The Wincondition switch (level 5) | Level 5. The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a passer drags defenders to passive squares, then a mating threat strikes the stripped king, or the reverse.
## Basic mates and mating technique [free] | endgame, basics | #endgame
- Basic mates: queen, rook and the ladder (level 1) | Level 1. The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
- Advanced mates and the Troitzky line (level 4) | Level 4. Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.
## Core principles and vocabulary [free] | endgame, basics | #endgame
- Core principles, typical errors and vocabulary (level 1) | Level 1. Once the queens are off the king becomes a fighting piece. These principles, the common errors and the vocabulary carry through every later level.
## The rule of the square and first passed pawns [free] | endgame, pawn-endgame | #endgame
- The rule of the square and your first passed pawns (level 1) | Level 1. A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.
## Opposition, key squares and tempo | endgame, pawn-endgame | #endgame
- Opposition and key squares (level 2) | Level 2. Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.
- Triangulation, shouldering and the Réti manoeuvre (level 3) | Level 3. Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
- Corresponding squares and mined squares (level 4) | Level 4. Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.
- Tempo parity, routes and domination (level 5) | Level 5. Tempo parity is global: count every spare move on the board, think in routes instead of single moves and take every square from a minor piece.
## Passed pawns, majorities and races | endgame, pawn-endgame | #endgame
- Outside, protected and separated passed pawns (level 2) | Level 2. A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
- Breakthroughs, majorities, tempi and rook pawns (level 3) | Level 3. Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
- Outside versus protected passers and the queening race (level 4) | Level 4. Calculate, do not quote slogans: compare how long the outside passer distracts the king with how long the protected passer ties it down.
- Passed pawns and majorities at master level (level 5) | Level 5. Advance your passers when it gains space or ties the opponent down, blockade theirs early, and use the majority on the wing the kings left.
## Rook endings | endgame, rook-endgame | #endgame
- Lucena and Philidor (level 2) | Level 2. Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
- The practical rook ending (level 3) | Level 3. Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
- The rook canon: Rule of Five, Vančura and the g7/h7 rule (level 4) | Level 4. The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.
- The grandmaster layer of rook endings (level 5) | Level 5. Activity can outweigh two pawns: the side that completes its triangle of active rook, active king and passer first usually wins.
## Queen endings | endgame, queen-endgame | #endgame
- Queen versus a pawn on the seventh (level 2) | Level 2. A queen usually stops a pawn on the seventh, but against bishop and rook pawns the stalemate tricks save the defender.
- Queen endings: winning zone, fortresses and cross-checks (level 4) | Level 4. The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.
- Queen and heavy-piece endings at master level (level 5) | Level 5. Queen endings are races of passers and checks; trust the position rather than the piece myth.
## Bishops, knights and the blockade | endgame, minor-piece-endgame | #endgame
- The wrong bishop and minor pieces against passed pawns (level 2) | Level 2. A bishop with a rook pawn only wins if it controls the promotion square, and minor pieces stop passers in different ways.
- Good bishop, bad bishop, bishop versus knight and the blockade (level 3) | Level 3. Pawns on the bishop's colour make it bad; knights love closed positions and blockade squares; knight endings behave like pawn endings.
- Knight, bishop and pawn endings (level 4) | Level 4. Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare, bishops need a diagonal across the pawn's path, and a knight can give itself up for the last pawn.
- Knight versus bad bishop and bishop versus knight (level 5) | Level 5. A knight against a bad bishop generates Winconditions by itself; with pawns on both wings, create a passer on one wing and invade on the other.
## Opposite-coloured bishops | endgame, minor-piece-endgame | #endgame
- Opposite-coloured bishops (level 3) | Level 3. Alone, opposite-coloured bishops are drawish even a pawn or two down; with rooks or queens they favour the attacker.
- Opposite-coloured bishops: the winning recipe (level 5) | Level 5. To win with opposite-coloured bishops you need two passers far apart; connected passers must reach the sixth rank.
## Rook versus minor pieces and material balance | endgame, minor-piece-endgame | #endgame
- Rook versus a minor piece: the corner decides (level 3) | Level 3. Without pawns a rook usually cannot beat a minor piece: the defender has to run to the right corner.
- Pawnless endings: 2B v N, R+B v R, queen v minor pieces (level 4) | Level 4. Tablebases overturned old verdicts: two bishops beat a knight, queen beats two bishops, but the 50-move rule can rescue the defender.
- Material by the numbers and up the exchange (level 5) | Level 5. Database numbers: bishop and knight are equal on average, the bishop pair is worth about half a pawn, rooks gain value as pawns disappear.
## Conversion, fortresses and exchanging | endgame, strategy | #endgame
- Converting an extra pawn (Tier 1 checklist) (level 2) | Level 2. Winning a pawn is step one of three: win it, turn it into a passer, escort it home. Calculate every trade into a pawn ending.
- Two weaknesses, do not hurry and the pawn-ending test (Tier 2 checklist) (level 3) | Level 3. One weakness can be defended, two cannot. When the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first.
- Fortresses, stalemate architecture and the 50-move horizon (Tier 3A checklist) (level 4) | Level 4. A fortress is a setup the attacker cannot break; stalemate can be a designed defence; theory and the 50-move rule can disagree.
- The art of exchanging (Tier 3B checklist) (level 5) | Level 5. Trade the defender's best piece, keep your best attacker, convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage and know what each exchange does.
## Planning, prophylaxis and the king | endgame, strategy | #endgame
- Planning, prophylaxis and the king (level 5) | Level 5. Picture the ideal setup first, ask what the opponent wants, improve your worst piece and restrict before you attack.
## Transformations and structure-born endgames | endgame, strategy | #endgame
- Transformations and structure-born endgames (level 5) | Level 5. Turn a static advantage into a dynamic one at the right moment, and know which endgames your middlegame structures leave behind.
## Fortress and anti-fortress | endgame, strategy | #endgame
- Fortress and anti-fortress (level 5) | Level 5. Test for fortresses before you simplify, know the warning signs and the toolkit for breaking them.
## Grandmaster technique | endgame, strategy | #endgame
- Grandmaster technique (level 5) | Level 5. Maximum problems for the opponent, minimum risk for you; repeat once, never three times; know tablebase metrics and build a personal anchor library.

think.title: The quiet queen move
think.brief: You're Black in the Caro-Kann. White just played 5.Qe2, a quiet move with a very loud idea.

stages.prompt: What did 5.Qe2 actually change?

options.text: The queen lines up with my king on the e-file, so my e7-pawn is pinned and no longer guards d6.
options.why: Exactly. e7 was the only piece covering d6, and now it can't move without exposing your king.

options.text: It prepares queenside castling and a pawn storm against my king.
options.why: Castling is a plan for later. Read what the move does right now: the queen is on the same file as your king.

options.text: It only defends the knight on e4 a second time.
options.why: It does defend e4, but that is the surface. The real change is behind your pieces, on the e-file.

stages.prompt: Tap the square White's knight wants to jump to.
stages.hint: Which squares can the e4-knight reach with check?
stages.explain: d6. Nd6 would be check, the only guard of d6 is the pinned e7-pawn, and your king is boxed in by its own pieces.

stages.prompt: Your natural developing move is 5...Ngf6. What is White's strongest reply to it?

options.text: 6.Nd6, and it is checkmate.
options.why: Checks first. d7 is blocked by your knight, e7 by the pinned pawn, d8 and f8 by your own pieces. Smothered.

options.text: 6.Nxf6+, a normal trade.
options.why: That's what you expect, not what White plays. Look at every check, not only the obvious one.

options.text: 6.Bg5, pinning the knight.
options.why: A decent developing move, but it misses the knockout. Checks, captures, attacks: in that order.

stages.prompt: Play the safe route. White's replies come automatically.

5...Ndf6.note: The d7-knight goes to f6. The d-file opens, so your queen now guards d6 as well: 6.Nd6+ would just lose a piece to ...Qxd6.

alt.e6: Also safe: the e-pawn steps off the pinned file.
alt.Qc7: Also safe: the queen covers d6 directly.

bad.Ngf6: 6.Nd6 is mate. The e7-pawn is pinned by the queen and your own knight on d7 blocks the king.

6...Nxf6.note: Recapture and you are out of the trap with a completely normal position.

7...Bg4.note: Pin the knight to the queen. White spent a tempo on Qe2 and achieved nothing.

debrief.t: 5.Qe2 put the queen on your king's file. That pinned e7, and e7 was the only guard of d6.
Your king had no free squares: d7, e7, d8 and f8 were all occupied by your own pieces.
Your opponent's CCAs matter as much as yours. Nd6 is a check, and after 5...Ngf6 it is mate.
5...Ndf6 opens the d-file so the queen guards d6. Calculate it: 6.Nd6+ Qxd6 and the trap is gone.

think.description: You're Black in the Caro-Kann. White just played 5.Qe2, a quiet move with a very loud idea.

ms_pc_breakdown.M: 5.Qe2 put the queen on your king's file. That pinned e7, and e7 was the only guard of d6.
ms_pc_breakdown.S: Your king had no free squares: d7, e7, d8 and f8 were all occupied by your own pieces.
ms_pc_breakdown.P: Your opponent's CCAs matter as much as yours. Nd6 is a check, and after 5...Ngf6 it is mate.
ms_pc_breakdown.C: 5...Ndf6 opens the d-file so the queen guards d6. Calculate it: 6.Nd6+ Qxd6 and the trap is gone.

think.explanation: It is completely normal to miss this one: 5.Qe2 looks like a quiet developing move. The loud part is hidden behind your own pieces, because the queen pins your e7-pawn and the knight on e4 is one jump from a smothered mate.
think.alarm_signal: ⚠️ ALARM SIGNAL / RED FLAG: When you see an enemy queen lined up on your king's file with only one pawn in between, plus an enemy knight that can jump to a check in your games, instantly ask yourself if a smothered mate that your natural developing move walks straight into is winning or necessary!
think.coaching_tip: 💡 Linked Course: Anti-Blunder Bootcamp: Read their threat first, and the Caro-Kann repertoire: Classical and the 5.Qe2 trap. Remember: Before every developing move, ask what the opponent's best CHECK is afterwards.

elo_insight.foundation: Foundation: look at every check your opponent has before you move. One scan saves the game.
elo_insight.advanced: Sharper: when your king has no flight squares, solve it with the move that gives the queen a guard of the key square (...Ndf6), not with the most natural one.

think.title: One pawn, two targets
think.brief: You are White in the Colle. Black released the tension with ...c4 and just played 9...b5 on the queenside.

stages.prompt: What does 9...b5 tell you?

options.text: Black is busy on the queenside and did nothing about my e4-e5 push.
options.why: Exactly. Black's bishop on d6 and knight on f6 still stand on the two squares a pawn on e5 would attack.

options.text: Black threatens ...b4 to win my c3-pawn, so I must defend first.
options.why: ...b4 is a plan, not a threat that needs an answer this move. Check what your own pawn can do first.

options.text: Black is preparing ...e5 to take over the centre.
options.why: ...e5 isn't on the board yet, and your e-pawn gets there first.

stages.prompt: Tap the square where one pawn would attack two pieces.
stages.hint: A pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6. What stands there?
stages.explain: e5. From there your pawn hits the d6-bishop and the f6-knight at once, and d4 protects it.

stages.prompt: Which CCA do you calculate first?

options.text: 10.e5, an attack on two pieces at once.
options.why: An attacking move that wins material by force. Black can only save one of the two pieces.

options.text: 10.exd5, a capture in the centre.
options.why: Captures are forcing, but this one wins nothing: 10...exd5 and the position is level.

options.text: 10.Qe2, developing and preparing Re1.
options.why: A good move in a normal position. Here it gives Black time for ...dxe4 or ...e5 and the fork disappears.

stages.prompt: Play the fork and collect the piece.

10.e5.note: The fork. d4 protects the pawn, so capturing on e5 only loses more material.

miss.Qe2: A sensible move in any other position, but e5 wins a piece right now.
miss.exd5: That releases the tension: after 10...exd5 the fork is gone for good.
miss.Re1: Too slow. The fork is available now and it will not come back.

11.exf6.note: Collect the knight. Black gets a pawn back with ...Nxf6 and you are a clean piece up.

think.title: MSPC drill: the smothered mate
think.brief: You are a piece down. The entire MSPC cycle on one position: read the move, name the specifics, list the CCAs, then calculate to the end.

stages.prompt: What does Black's setup tell you?

options.text: The king on h8 has no escape squares: g7 and h7 are his own pawns
options.why: That is the feature the whole combination runs on. A king with no flight squares is a mating target, not a safe king.

options.text: Black is threatening ...Qxb2 and you must defend
options.why: Defending is exactly the reflex MSPC is built to stop. Read the position first: your attack is faster.

options.text: Black's extra piece means you should trade into an endgame
options.why: Trading when you are material down just loses more slowly. Look for the forcing line first.

stages.prompt: Tap the square both your queen and your knight can reach.
stages.hint: Your queen sits on the a2-g8 diagonal and your knight is on g5.
stages.explain: f7 is the intersection. The c4-queen covers it through d5 and e6, and the g5-knight jumps there with check.

stages.prompt: Which CCA do you calculate first?

options.text: Nf7+, because a check with the knight forces the king to a square you choose
options.why: Checks first. Forcing moves narrow the opponent's replies to almost nothing, which is what makes deep calculation possible.

options.text: Qxc6, because a capture wins material back
options.why: It wins a knight and loses the game to ...Qxb2 and counterplay. Checks come before captures when the king is boxed in.

options.text: Rd1, because an attacking move improves the worst piece
options.why: Slow moves come last. There is a forced mate on the board.

stages.prompt: Play the forced mate. Black's replies come automatically.

1.Nf7+.note: Check one. The king must go to g8 — the rook on e8 cannot capture and g7/h7 are blocked.

2.Nh6+.note: Double check from the knight and the queen together. Only the king may move, and 2...Kf8 runs into 3.Qf7 mate.

3.Qg8+.note: The queen sacrifice. It is not a sacrifice — it is a deflection: the rook is dragged onto g8 where it blocks the king's last square.

4.Nf7#.note: Philidor's Legacy. The king is smothered by his own pieces.

debrief.t: The king on h8 is walled in by g7 and h7 — no escape squares means mate patterns are live.
Your queen owns the a2-g8 diagonal, the knight has f7 and h6, and the black rook on e8 is one square from g8.
Checks, captures, attacks — and here the check is the move that keeps every reply forced.
Four moves, every one a check, so no calculation cutoff: at each step there was only one legal reply to consider.

think.title: MSPC drill: overloaded defender
think.brief: You are a bishop down and the black back rank is one move from collapse. Find the deflection.

stages.prompt: What has Black's play left behind?

options.text: Black never made luft: the king on g8 has no escape square.
options.why: That is the weakness everything else builds on. Three unmoved pawns in front of a king are a wall and a trap at the same time.

options.text: Black threatens ...Qd1+ with a back-rank mate of his own.
options.why: d1 is covered by your rook and your knight. Your back rank holds. The question is whether Black's does.

options.text: The bishop on b7 is loose, so I should attack it.
options.why: It is loose, but it is a slow target. Look for something forcing first.

stages.prompt: Tap Black's overloaded piece.
stages.hint: Which black piece is the only defender of the rook on e8?
stages.explain: The d8-queen is the sole defender of e8. An overloaded defender is the first thing to look for once you spot a weak back rank.

stages.prompt: Which forcing move do you check first?

options.text: Qxe8+, deflecting the queen onto e8
options.why: Take the defender's job away by force. After ...Qxe8 the queen is standing on the square she was defending.

options.text: Nd5, threatening to jump into e7
options.why: Black simply defends. A quiet threat gives the opponent a move; the back rank will be repaired with ...h6.

options.text: Re7, attacking along the seventh
options.why: The rook on e8 covers e7. Checks and captures come before attacking moves.

stages.prompt: Play it out.

1.Qxe8+.note: The queen is forced to recapture: the king cannot take, and no other black piece reaches e8.

2.Rxe8#.note: Back-rank mate. The pawns on f7, g7 and h7 that looked like a wall were the reason the king had nowhere to go.

debrief.t: Black never spent a move on ...h6, so the back rank has been a standing weakness the whole game.
One defender (the queen), one entry square (e8), one open file — that combination is what deflection tactics feed on.
Qxe8+ is both a check and a capture: the most forcing move available, so it is calculated first.
Two moves deep, but you must see to the end: the value of the queen is irrelevant once the line finishes in mate.

think.title: Remove the guard
think.brief: You are Black in the Advance with 3...c5. Everything you have done is aimed at d4. White just asked your bishop a question with 8.h3.

stages.prompt: What did 8.h3 do?

options.text: It attacks my bishop on g4, and does nothing for d4.
options.why: Right. A move that attacks one thing and defends nothing else gives you a free hand. Your bishop has to move or take, so make that move count.

options.text: It defends d4 a third time.
options.why: Look again: the h-pawn only touches g4. d4 has exactly the same defenders as before.

options.text: It prepares g4 and a kingside attack.
options.why: Your king isn't even castled. Read the concrete threat first: it's aimed at the bishop.

stages.prompt: Tap the pawn this whole position revolves around.
stages.hint: Your c5-pawn, your c6-knight and your b6-queen all point at the same square.
stages.explain: d4. You attack it three times (c5, Nc6, Qb6) and White defends it three times: c3, the f3-knight and the d1-queen. Remove one defender and it falls.

stages.prompt: Which CCA starts the win of d4?

options.text: 8...Bxf3, capturing a defender first.
options.why: Captures first, and the right capture: after Bxf3 the knight is gone and d4 has two defenders left against your three attackers.

options.text: 8...cxd4, taking on d4 straight away.
options.why: Your bishop is still hanging: 9.hxg4 and you've lost a piece. Deal with the attacked piece and the target in one move.

options.text: 8...Bh5, keeping the pin.
options.why: Solid but slow. White gets time for Be3 or dxc5 and d4 is safe again. The initiative was yours to take.

stages.prompt: Collect the pawn. Check White's counterplay at every step.

8...Bxf3.note: The guard is gone. d4 now has two defenders against three attackers.

9...cxd4.note: Now take. The c-file opens and d4 is about to fall.

10...Qxd4.note: The queen takes: centralised, and a clean pawn up.

bad.Nxd4: Natural, but 11.Bxd5! wins the pawn back: White has just enough activity. Take with the queen and the extra pawn stays.

11...Nxd4.note: A healthy extra pawn in the endgame, and the knight hits the f3-bishop. This is what pressure on d4 is for.

debrief.t: 8.h3 attacked the bishop and did nothing else. A one-job move gives you a free hand.
Advance structure: d4 is the base of White's pawn chain, the square your whole setup (...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6) is built to attack.
Count attackers and defenders: three against three. Capturing a defender with Bxf3 turns it into three against two.
Calculate to the end, including counterplay: 10...Nxd4? 11.Bxd5! hands the pawn back, while 10...Qxd4 keeps it.

think.title: When Black forks first
think.brief: You’re White in your Colle-Koltanowski. After 10.Qe2, Black didn’t wait: 10...dxe4.

stages.prompt: What did 10...dxe4 change?

options.text: The pawn on e4 attacks my bishop on d3 and my knight on f3 at the same time.
options.why: Exactly. A pawn fork: unless you recapture, one of the two pieces is lost.

options.text: It only opens the d-file for Black’s rooks.
options.why: The d-file matters later. Right now that pawn attacks two of your pieces.

options.text: Nothing urgent. I can play Re1 first and take back later.
options.why: Then 11...exf3 wins a piece. Read what the move attacks before you follow your own plan.

stages.prompt: Apart from the king, only one black piece defends h7. Tap it.
stages.hint: Which black piece can reach h7 in one move?
stages.explain: The f6-knight. Trade it off and your Bd3 and Qe2 both point straight at h7.

stages.prompt: Which recapture keeps the advantage?

options.text: 11.Nxe4: it recaptures and offers to trade the f6-knight.
options.why: Right. After 11...Nxe4 your queen or bishop recaptures on the b1-h7 diagonal, aiming at h7.

options.text: 11.Bxe4: take back with the bishop.
options.why: 11...Nxe4 12.Nxe4 and your light-squared bishop is gone. The pressure on h7 disappears with it.

options.text: 11.Bc2: save the bishop first.
options.why: 11...exf3 wins the knight. A fork has to be answered with a capture or a check.

stages.prompt: Play it out. Black’s replies come automatically.

11.Nxe4.note: The capture that answers the fork and offers to trade Black’s best defender.

11...Nxe4.note: Black trades, and the f6-knight is gone.

12.Qxe4.note: Queen and bishop line up on h7. The threat is 13.Qxh7 mate.

alt.Bxe4: Also good: the bishop recaptures and keeps aiming at h7. The course line takes with the queen to force a concession.

12...f5.note: The only defence. 12...Bd7?? 13.Qxh7 is mate, and after 12...Re8 13.Qxh7+ White wins.

13.Qc4.note: The queen steps away from the f5-pawn and eyes e6 and the c5-bishop. After ...f5, e6 stays weak for the rest of the game.

alt.Qe2: Playable too. Qc4 keeps more pressure on e6 and c5.
alt.Qh4: Playable too, but Qc4 is more precise.

Only the f6-knight defended h7. Trading it turned your Bd3 and Qe2 into an attack.

After 12.Qxe4 Black had exactly one defence, 12...f5, and it left e6 weak for the rest of the game.

think.brief: You’re Black in your Meran. White skipped castling and pushed 9.e4 straight away.

stages.prompt: What did 9.e4 change?

options.text: White threatens e4-e5, kicking my f6-knight away from the centre.
options.why: Right. The pawn wants e5, and from there it hits your best defender.

options.text: It only builds a big centre. Nothing is threatened yet.
options.why: Read it as a threat: next move e4-e5 hits the f6-knight.

options.text: It prepares queenside castling.

stages.prompt: Tap the square White’s pawn wants to reach next move.

options.text: 9...Qa5, pinning the c3-knight.
options.why: It pins the knight, but e4-e5 still comes with tempo against f6.

options.text: 9...c5, striking in the centre immediately.
options.why: 10.e5 attacks f6 before your central counter-strike takes effect.

stages.prompt: Play 9...b4 and force White to react.

9...b4.note: Attacks c3 before White can play e5.

10...e5.note: Strikes at the centre while White's knight is out of position.

think.title: Bishop out before ...e6: the point of the Advance
think.brief: You are Black in the Caro-Kann Advance. White has just released the tension with 6.cxd4, and the pawns on d4 and e5 now form a chain. Your c8-bishop is still outside that chain. Decide what to do with it before the structure closes.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 6.cxd4 change in the structure?

options.text: It released the pawn tension: White now has a d4-e5 chain and the c-file is open, while my c8-bishop is still outside the chain.
options.why: Correct. The move fixed the structure. Read the structure first, because it tells you which of your pieces is the problem piece and which one is free.

options.text: It threatens d4xd5, winning my central pawn.
options.why: A pawn captures diagonally. The d4-pawn attacks c5 and e5, and my d5-pawn stands straight in front of it. Nothing is threatened.

options.text: It attacks my knight on c6 and forces it to move.
options.why: The d4-pawn does not attack c6. Check what each pawn really attacks before you react to a threat that is not there.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the square where the c8-bishop pins the f3-knight against the queen. This is the repertoire square.
stages.hint: Which square on the c8-h3 diagonal puts the bishop in front of the pawn chain and in line with f3 and d1?
stages.explain: g4. The bishop leaves the French-type trap before ...e6 is played, and the pin on f3 targets the knight that defends d4 and e5.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan of this structure?

options.text: 6...Bg4: develop the problem bishop with a pin first, then play ...e6.
options.why: Correct. Bishop out first, then ...e6. That order is the rule for your whole repertoire.

options.text: 6...e6: complete the French structure at once.
options.why: This is the move the course warns against. After ...e6 the bishop is locked behind its own pawn chain and you have an Advance French a tempo down.

options.text: 6...Qb6: hit d4 and b2 straight away.
options.why: It attacks two pawns but develops nothing, and the problem bishop is still shut in. A slow plan with a lost tempo is not what this structure asks for.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

6...Bg4.note: The bishop is out before ...e6. In the French this piece is Black's problem; here it is solved on move six.

alt.Bf5: Also playable: the bishop is outside the chain as well. The repertoire move is Bg4 because it pins the f3-knight and so pressures d4.

bad.e6: Locks the bishop in. This is the whole variation thrown away.

7.Be2.note: White breaks the pin by developing the bishop to e2.

7...e6.note: Now the French structure is built, with the good bishop already outside.

8.O-O.note: White castles. Nothing is forcing yet.

8...Nge7.note: The knight goes to e7, not f6, and the next detail shows why.

bad.Nf6: 9.exf6. The e5-pawn attacks f6, so the knight would simply be lost.

9...Nf5.note: The knight reaches f5. Pawns cannot drive it away, and it adds a second attacker to d4.

10.Be3.note: White defends d4 with the bishop.

10...Be7.note: Black finishes development. The target is d4, and White has no way to attack the structure.

debrief.t: 6.cxd4 settled the pawn structure: a d4-e5 chain for White and an open c-file. Name the structure before you move.
The specific feature is the unlocked bishop. In the French it is a problem piece behind ...e6. Here it can still reach g4 or f5 outside the chain, and from g4 it pins the knight on f3.
Priority: develop the problem piece first. 6...Bg4 comes before ...e6, and the order is the rule for the whole repertoire.
Calculate the one tactical point: ...Nf6 is not available because e5xf6, so the knight must go to e7 and then f5. 8...Nge7 9.Nc3 Nf5 reaches the target square without a tactical flaw.

The plan: bishop out, then ...e6, ...Nge7-f5 and pressure on d4. White's d4-pawn needs Nc3, Be3 and Qd2 to hold it, so he has no time for a kingside plan, and his only active try is g4 to chase the f5-knight, which weakens his own king. The honest assessment: this is equal, and the plan gives a comfortable game rather than a forced win.

think.title: The Greek gift: check the three conditions, then play Bxh7+
think.brief: You are White in the Colle-Koltanowski. You have played e4-e5, kicked the f6-knight away, and Black has just retreated his bishop to f8, where it covers the king. The famous sacrifice on h7 is in the air. Do not play it from habit: check the conditions first.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 12...Bf8 change?

options.text: 13.Bxh7+: the Greek gift. Black's knight has left f6, your knight can reach g5 with check and the queen can join.

options.text: 13.Nbd4: trade knights and keep the pieces coordinated.

The plan: use the Greek gift when three things are true. Black's knight has left f6, your knight can jump to g5 with check, and your queen can join quickly. The attack is hard to stop because the black king is pulled out, the pieces that could defend are on the wrong side of the board, and every defensive move that loosens the position gives White a new check. The honest assessment: White is close to winning here, but only because all three conditions are met. The same sacrifice without the three conditions is a blunder.

think.title: Koltanowski's method: recapture towards the isolated pawn
think.brief: You are White in the Colle. The exchanges in the centre have left Black with an isolated pawn on d5, and he has just played ...Nxf3+ with check. You have two ways to recapture. One keeps your plan alive, the other destroys it.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 15...Nxf3+ do?

options.text: It is a check that also attacks my rook on e1, so I must recapture on f3 immediately.
options.why: Correct. The knight gives check and attacks the rook, so you cannot ignore it. The only question is which piece recaptures.

options.text: It is a quiet developing move, so I can continue with my own plan.
options.why: It is a check. A check has to be answered, and the knight also attacks the rook on e1.

options.text: It wins my h3-pawn.
options.why: The knight on f3 does not attack h3. It attacks the king, the rook on e1 and other squares.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap Black's isolated pawn, the target of your whole plan.
stages.hint: Black has no pawn on the c-file or the e-file next to it.
stages.explain: d5. The pawn has no neighbours to defend it, so it needs a constant piece defence. You blockade it, trade minor pieces and attack it with more pieces than defend it.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which recapture keeps the plan alive?

options.text: 16.Qxf3: recapture with the queen, keep the structure and play against the isolated pawn.
options.why: Correct. White always recaptures towards a position with an isolated pawn for Black, where Black lacks real activity.

options.text: 16.gxf3: recapture with the pawn.
options.why: It doubles your pawns and opens the g-file against your own king, and after 16...Bxh3 Black wins a pawn as well. You go from clearly better to clearly worse.

options.text: 16.Kh1: step out of the check and keep the rook.
options.why: 16...Nxe1 wins the exchange. Much weaker than Qxf3: it throws the advantage away.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. Black's replies come automatically.

16.Qxf3.note: Koltanowski's own method: force the exchanges and play against the isolated d5-pawn. The plan never changes, at every level.

bad.gxf3: Doubled pawns, a weakened king and 16...Bxh3 wins a pawn. It throws away the structure you are playing for.
bad.Kh1: 16...Nxe1 and White has lost the exchange.

16...Be6.note: Black develops the bishop to the only reasonable square.

17.Be3.note: You develop and cover d4. Next you want to blockade the isolated pawn.

17...Rad8.note: Black puts a rook behind the isolated pawn.

18.Bc2.note: The bishop keeps the b1-h7 diagonal. Even in quiet positions that diagonal stays alive, so keep this bishop.

debrief.t: 15...Nxf3+ is a check and attacks the rook on e1. You must recapture, and the choice of piece fixes the structure.
Specific feature: Black has an isolated pawn on d5. His light-squared bishop has no good square, and your bishop on e4 or c2 stays on the long diagonal.
Priority: the structure. Qxf3 keeps your pawns healthy and leaves Black with the isolated pawn; gxf3 would damage your own.
Calculate the other recaptures: 16.gxf3? hands over your structure, and 16.Kh1? loses the exchange to 16...Nxe1.

The plan: blockade the isolated pawn with a piece, trade minor pieces, and keep the bishop for the b1-h7 diagonal in case a sacrifice appears. Black cannot free himself because every pawn break loses the d5-pawn or opens the position for your better pieces, so he is left defending passively. The honest assessment: White has a small but stable edge, the kind that grows slowly if you keep your structure healthy. Queens being on is not the point: the structure is.

think.title: Take on f6 and keep Black passive
think.brief: You are White in the Colle. Your e5-pawn has cramped Black, your bishop on d4 dominates the long diagonal, and Black has just played ...f6 to challenge the wedge. Decide how to respond.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 15...f6 do?

options.text: It challenges the e5-pawn with a pawn and opens the f-file; I must decide whether to take.
options.why: Correct. The pawn on e5 is attacked by f6 and defended by the bishop and the knight, so you decide how the structure changes.

options.text: It threatens ...fxe5 winning a piece.
options.why: The pawn on e5 is defended twice, by the bishop on d4 and the knight on f3. After ...fxe5 you simply recapture.

options.text: It attacks my bishop on d4.
options.why: The f6-pawn attacks e5 and g5. Check what each pawn really attacks.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.why: Correct. Take and keep Black without counterplay. That keeps White clearly better.

options.text: 16.Bxh7+: cash in the sacrifice.
options.why: 16...Kxh7 17.exf6 Nxf6 and you have given a bishop for a pawn. Black comes out clearly ahead after this, so it is a mistake. The sacrifice has nothing behind it here.

options.text: 16.Bc2: retreat and keep the bishop.

bad.Bxh7+: 16...Kxh7 17.exf6 Nxf6 and you are a piece down for a pawn.

debrief.t: 15...f6 challenges the wedge on e5. The pawn is defended twice, so there is no tactical danger.

The plan: pressure e6 with the rooks and queen, use the e5-square for a knight or bishop and improve slowly. Black is left with no counterplay at all, because his pieces are tied to the defence of e6 and his only pawn break, ...c5 or ...f5, is no longer available. The value of this line is not the size of the advantage but its nature: it converts far more often than a speculative attack. The honest assessment: White is clearly better here, and the edge comes from the structure, not from a risky attack.

think.title: Meet e4 with ...b4: counter before e5 forks
think.brief: You are Black in the Meran at Advanced depth. White has played 13.e4 and threatens to push the pawn to e5. You must counter at once with a pawn move on the queenside, otherwise a fork follows.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 13.e4 threaten?

options.text: e4-e5, forking my bishop on d6 and my knight on f6.
options.why: Correct. A pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6 at once. This is the threat you must meet.

options.text: e4xd5, winning a pawn.
options.why: There is no pawn on d5 for the e4-pawn to capture.

options.text: Nothing yet: it only claims space.
options.why: It is a real threat: e5 forks two pieces. Read the threat first.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the White knight that the pawn on b4 will attack.
stages.hint: Your b-pawn can attack it from b4.
stages.explain: c3. The knight on c3 supports the push to e5. Attack it with ...b4 and the structure changes before e5 comes.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move meets the threat with a counter-threat?

options.text: 13...b4: attack the knight on c3 first.
options.why: Correct. A counter-threat that deflects the knight before e5 can be played.

options.text: 13...Be7: retreat the bishop out of the fork.
options.why: 14.e5 attacks the knight, and after 14...Nd5 15.Bxh7+ White wins material. Clearly weaker than ...b4.

options.text: 13...c5: strike in the centre at once.
options.why: It leaves the b5-pawn undefended: 14.Bxb5 wins a pawn. Clearly weaker than ...b4.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

13...b4.note: Attack the knight on c3 before White can play e5.

bad.Be7: 14.e5 attacks the knight and after 14...Nd5 15.Bxh7+ White wins material.
bad.c5: Leaves the b5-pawn undefended: 14.Bxb5 wins a pawn.

14...axb4.note: Black recaptures and keeps the pawn on b4.

15.e5.note: White pushes the pawn and forks the bishop and the knight.

15...bxc3.note: Black takes the knight on c3 first.

17...Bxf3.note: Black takes the knight on f3. The position is equal and very sharp.

debrief.t: 13.e4 threatens e5, which forks the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6.
Specific feature: the c3-knight supports the push, and my b-pawn can attack it from b4.
Priority: a counter-threat. 13...b4 meets the threat with a threat.
Calculate the main line: 14.axb4 axb4 15.e5 bxc3 16.exd6 c5 17.dxc5 Bxf3 leads to a sharp, balanced position. 13...Be7? loses material to 14.e5 and 13...c5? loses the b5-pawn.

The plan: use the tactical resource ...b4 to deflect the knight and then play ...c5. This is a sharp line, so the moves must be known. The honest assessment: the position is level, and the whole point is the timing of ...b4. The point is the timing, not a long-term pawn structure.

think.title: Deflect the knight with ...b4, then strike with ...c5
think.brief: You are Black in a Master-level Meran. You have played ...Rc8 and ...b4, and White has retreated his knight to a4. The knight on a4 now eyes c5, the square of your central break.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 13.Na4 change?

options.text: The knight retreated from c3 and now eyes c5, so my central break looks prevented.
options.why: Correct. The knight on a4 covers c5 and b6. Check what the retreat attacks before you continue.

options.text: It attacks my bishop on d6.
options.why: The knight on a4 does not attack d6. It attacks b6, c5, b2 and c3.

options.text: It forks my queen and my rook.
options.why: The knight on a4 attacks b6, c5, c3 and b2. There is no fork on my queen and rook.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the square of your central break.
stages.hint: The pawn on c6 wants to advance.
stages.explain: c5. The break has been prepared by ...b4, which pulled the knight to a4. The pattern is: ...b4 first to deflect the knight, then ...c5.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.text: 13...c5: strike at once, now that the knight has been deflected.
options.why: Correct. This is the key resource of the structure: ...b4 first, then ...c5.

options.text: 13...a5: support the b4-pawn.
options.why: It is too slow and White consolidates. Clearly weaker than ...c5.

options.text: 13...bxa3: take the pawn.
options.why: It opens the b-file for White and gives up the pressure. Clearly weaker than ...c5.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

13...c5.note: The key resource. The knight was deflected by ...b4, and now ...c5 hits the centre.

bad.bxa3: Gives up the pressure and opens the b-file for White.

14...Nxc5.note: Black recaptures with the knight and is fine.

debrief.t: 13.Na4 retreated the knight and covers c5, but it is no longer on c3.
Specific feature: the knight was deflected from c3 by ...b4, and the c5-break is the key square of the structure.
Priority: strike while the knight is offside. 13...c5 uses the deflection.
Calculate the alternatives: 13...a5? is too slow and 13...bxa3? gives up the pressure. After 14.dxc5 Nxc5 Black is fine.

The plan: deflect the knight with ...b4, strike with ...c5, and use the open lines and the bishop on b7. White's knight on a4 is badly placed, so the pawn break wins time. The honest assessment: Black is clearly better here, but this is a concrete resource, not a general rule. Know the pattern and check the position each time.

ms_pc_breakdown.M: Black just played: Rxd6 captured a pawn on d6, so material and structure just shifted; it now attacks your rook on d5. Ask yourself what that rook left behind on d8, and which square it no longer covers.

ms_pc_breakdown.M: Black just played: Rc6 repositioned the rook from c8 to c6; it now attacks your bishop on d3. Ask yourself what that rook left behind on c8, and which square it no longer covers.
ms_pc_breakdown.S: You are behind by about a rook on paper, so the board has to give you something concrete (queen, rook, bishop and knight against queen, two rooks, bishop and knight). Your opponent has a passed pawn on d4 (his 5th rank). The enemy king has only 1 free square to run to. A king with few flight squares and loose checks around it is the signature of a mating net.
ms_pc_breakdown.P: Your CCA list: 7 checks and 2 captures. The key move, Qh7+, is a check, so it goes to the top of the list and keeps the opponent's replies limited.
ms_pc_breakdown.C: Calculate it to the end: 30. Qh7+ Rxh7 31. Rg4+ Kh8 32. Rg8#. After your first move your opponent has only 2 legal replies; check each one. The line ends in checkmate. Can you say in one sentence why the other defences fail?

middlegame.explanation: The enemy king has almost no room, so a short run of forcing moves finishes it before the defence can react.
middlegame.alarm_signal: ⚠️ ALARM SIGNAL / RED FLAG: When you see an enemy king with only 1 free square left and a rook one check away from the finish in your games, instantly ask yourself if a forcing check that takes the last escape square (mate in 3 here) is winning or necessary!
middlegame.coaching_tip: 💡 Linked Course: The Middlegame Masterclass, chapter 3B.1 (Prophylaxis Masterclass: Overprotection, Restraint, Preventing Counterplay). Remember: Before any quiet move, count the enemy king's free squares: if there are two or fewer, search every check first.

elo_insight.foundation: Foundation: with a king boxed in, list ALL your checks. One of them may be mate.
elo_insight.advanced: Sharper: make sure your last check cannot be blocked or captured, and that no move in the line stalemates the king.

bridge.title: Knight on e5: build the wedge (vs the fianchetto)
bridge.summary: Black has fianchettoed and nobody contests e5. Your knight is already there: now you back it up.
plan: Beginner: Pile onto e5: Ne5, f4, Bd3, Qe2 or Qc2. Never trade the e5 knight voluntarily.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Challenge e5 directly with ...Nc6 or ...Nd7-f6 pressure, or prepare ...f6.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: Black has to attack e5 to get counterplay and he has nothing to attack it with once ...g6/...Bg7 is missing. Every ...f5, ...g6 or ...h6 loosens the dark squares f6-g6-h6 for good, so his kingside gets weaker with each move he spends on defence. This is not a forced win: the position stays roughly level, and the point is a durable plan with a clean fallback in minor-piece endings.
bridge.mistake: Trade the e5 knight voluntarily to simplify the position.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the e5-structure, and why?

accept.f4: Correct. The knight needs a pawn chain, not just a good square. f4 turns a temporary outpost into a permanent one.

alt.b3: Also playable: 8.b3 is almost as good as 8.f4. The choice is about the plan, not a tactic. f4 is the repertoire move because it commits to the e5 structure.

bad.Qe2: The e3-pawn blocks the queen from e5, so the knight still has only d4 behind it. Flexible is not the same as forcing.
bad.Ndf3: It does guard e5, but it blocks your own f-pawn, so f4 can never arrive. You trade the outpost wedge for a passive set-up.

bridge.title: Pawn wedge on e5 (vs ...Nbd7)
bridge.summary: Black has traded on e5 and recaptured so that your d-pawn stands on e5. The wedge is a pawn this time.
plan: Beginner: Pile onto e5: Ne5, f4, Bd3, Qe2 or Qc2. Never trade the e5 knight voluntarily.
Intermediate: Use g4-g5 to dislodge a defending ...Nf6, and aim rooks at the e- and f-files instead of rushing.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Avoid an early ...cxd4: it opens the long diagonal and e-file exactly when White wants them. ...f5 blunts the light-squared bishop.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: Black has to attack e5 to get counterplay and he has nothing to attack it with once ...g6/...Bg7 is missing. bridge.mistake: Trade the e5 knight voluntarily to simplify the position.

drill.prompt: Which move supports the wedge on e5, and why?

accept.f4: Correct. Here 10.f4 is clearly the most accurate move: the alternatives leave Black with an easier game.

bad.Bxh7+: No knight can reach g5 with tempo: your f3-knight was traded on e5. The sacrifice has only the queen behind it and Black simply takes.
bad.Qc2: It does not defend e5, so 10...Nxe5 wins a pawn and the knight hits your bishop on d3 at once.

bridge.title: Rook or bishop? The recapture on e4
bridge.summary: After the exchanges on e4 you decide how to recapture. The rook is the repertoire move and the reason Re1 was played.
plan: Beginner: Complete the manoeuvre Re1, e4, Rxe4, Rh4, aiming a Qd3/Qc2 + Rh4 + Ng5 battery at h7.
Intermediate: Keep Bd3 trained on h7 throughout. Avoid trades that let Black consolidate before the lift is complete.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Trade White's attacking minor pieces (the bishop on d3, the knight heading for g5) wherever offered.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: after 12.Rxe4 your rook, bishop and queen all point at h7 while Black's pieces are still unfinished, and each natural-looking Black move adds a defender that is too slow. 13.Rh4 creates a lasting initiative, while the quiet 13.Re1 leaves you with hardly anything. The honest limit: if ...h6 and ...Nf6 are both in place the rook is offside, so keep the central Plan B ready.
bridge.mistake: Rush the rook to h4 even when ...h6 and a knight on f6 are both already in place.

drill.prompt: Which recapture forces the rook-lift structure, and why?

accept.Rxe4: Correct. 12.Rxe4 keeps noticeably more pressure than 12.Bxe4. This is why Re1 was played.

bad.Bxe4: It gives a normal, slightly dull position and the rook stays passive on e1. It is a legitimate fallback, not the plan.

bridge.title: Greek gift: the conditions are met
bridge.summary: Black's knight has left f6 and nothing covers g5. Check the three conditions, then strike.
plan: Beginner: Know the mechanics cold: Bxh7+ Kxh7 Ng5+ then Qh5 (or Qg4), with mate threats on h7/h8 depending on king placement.
Intermediate: Recognise when the sacrifice is unsound (Black keeps ...Nf6 covering g5/h5, or has an in-between ...Qxg5) and do not force it.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Know the defensive geometry after the sacrifice (...Kg8 and ...Nf8 rerouting) well enough to survive an unsound try over the board.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the sacrifice is only on when three conditions meet: a knight that reaches g5 with tempo, a queen that joins at once, and no black knight on f6 to guard g5/h5/h7. When they do, Black's king is dragged into the open before his pieces can follow. In the two verified model positions White is clearly better, and in one of them close to winning. When any condition is missing, play Qc2/Re1 first and fall back on the slower plans.
bridge.mistake: Sacrifice on h7 whenever the bishop can, even when a knight on f6 or an in-between ...Qxg5 refutes it.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.Bxh7+: Correct. Here the sacrifice is clearly stronger than the best quiet alternative. The key detail is that Black's knight has left f6.

bad.Nbd4: It is a sound developing move, but it gives Black the one tempo he needs for ...h6, which is the cure for the whole sacrifice.
bad.Bf4: It spends a tempo on the wrong bishop: the attack lives on Bd3, Nf3 and the queen, not on the c1-bishop.

bridge.title: The isolani tabiya: put a piece on e5
bridge.summary: You hold the isolated d4-pawn. The plan is activity: bishops on e5, rooks on the open files, and the attack on h7.
plan: Beginner: Keep pieces on. Centralise the rooks on the c- and e-files and put a piece on e5.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Survive the middlegame without weakening your king just to dodge the initiative. It is provisional and fades naturally.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the isolani is a debt you repay with activity, and the debt is only collected if the pieces stay on. Black's best answer is to trade and blockade d5, so you must keep the initiative every move. In the verified model position White is winning, and a full-width mate search confirms that after 17.Qg5 Bd7 18.Rxh7 every Black reply loses to mate in at most four more White moves. Black's queen on a5 is out of the defence: that is the structural reason the plan cannot be parried.
bridge.mistake: Trade pieces to reach a calm ending: every trade shrinks the attack while the weakness stays.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.Be5: Correct. Both 16.Be5 and 16.Bc7 are winning here. The IQP rewards activity.

alt.Bc7: Also winning here. The repertoire move is Be5 because it keeps the bishop central and the plan simple.

bad.Qe3: Every trade shrinks your attack while the isolated pawn stays. Trading queens is exactly what Black wants.

bridge.title: Tartakower: Re8 before anything else
bridge.summary: After the knights are traded you recapture with the e-pawn. The regrouping starts with ...Re8.
plan: Beginner: Standard regrouping: Bd6, O-O, Re8, Nd7-f8, Be6, Qd7.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Use the open e-file (Re1) and aim pressure at the e6/e5 complex.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the open e-file, active pieces and the ...f5 lever are your compensation, and the regrouping Bd6, O-O, Re8, Nd7-f8, Be6, Qd7 is textbook. Both sides keep both bishops, so you do not own the bishop pair. The honest limit: keep queens and heavy pieces on, because mass simplification turns the structure into a liability.
bridge.mistake: Trade down into a pure ending: the doubled f-pawns are a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.Re8: Correct. ...Bg4 is slightly more accurate, so both are playable; ...Re8 is the repertoire move.

alt.Bg4: Also playable, and slightly more accurate. ...Re8 is the repertoire move because it provokes h3.

bad.Bf5: 7...Bf5?? is answered by Bxf5 and your light-squared bishop is gone: the structure needs it for the ...Bxh3 idea.

bridge.title: Panov: survive the initiative
bridge.summary: White has an isolated d4. Do not weaken your king to dodge his initiative: it is provisional.
plan: Beginner: Survive the middlegame without weakening your king just to avoid White's initiative: the initiative is provisional and fades naturally.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Keep pieces on the board: an IQP wants activity, not trades. Centralise rooks and put a knight on e5.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: White's initiative is provisional and fades with every trade, while the structural weakness stays. You blockade d5 with a knight, trade attackers and, after ...Bxc3 bxc3, you aim at d4 and c3 at the same time. The reference positions give Black a small, comfortable edge. Once queens are off the position is often technically winning for the defender.

bridge.title: Caro Exchange: the bishop before ...e6
bridge.summary: The structure is symmetrical. Develop the bishop first and meet Qb3 with Qd7.
plan: Beginner: Mirror normal development: bishop out (...Bg4/...Bf5) before ...e6, then ...Nc6 and ...Nf6.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Use the half-open e-file (Re1), normal development (Bd3, Nf3, O-O) and never assume it is an automatic draw.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: you hold the queenside minority, so ...b5-b4 is your pawn plan, and ...e5 breaks the symmetry when the tactics allow it. White keeps a slight edge: treat this as an equal, practical structure and avoid passive mirroring.
bridge.mistake: Assume the symmetrical structure is an automatic draw and mirror White passively.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.Bg4: Correct. 6...Bg4 is the best move, even though White keeps a slight edge. The structure is equal, not better for Black.

bad.e6: Develop your light bishop before ...e6: the bishop on c8 is the piece that gets buried.

bridge.title: Doubled g-pawns: the accepting chair

endgame.title: Rule of the square: catch the b-pawn

1.Ke3.note: Enters the square of the b-pawn, so the king catches it. With Black to move, 1...b3 would have promoted: the side to move decides this position. Draw.

3.Kc2.note: The pawn falls next move; only the two kings are left, a dead position.

courses.endgame.title: The laws that decide endgames (level 1)
courses.endgame.idea: Before technique, know when a game is already over: stalemate, dead position, repetition, the 50-move rule, flag-fall and the free choice of promotion piece.
courses.endgame.takeaway: A won position is only won if you do not stalemate, repeat or run out of time.
learn: Before technique, know when a game is already over: stalemate, dead position, repetition, the 50-move rule, flag-fall and the free choice of promotion piece.
R0.1 (Law). Stalemate is a draw. The side to move has no legal move and is not in check.
R0.2 (Law). Dead position = immediate draw. When neither side can checkmate by any series of legal moves — K vs K, K+B vs K, K+N vs K, K+B vs K+B with same-coloured bishops — the game ends drawn.

R0.3 (Law). Repetition. A draw can be claimed when the same position occurs for the third time (same player to move, same castling and en passant rights). The fifth occurrence ends the game automatically.

R0.4 (Law). The 50-move rule. 50 moves by each player without a capture or a pawn move: a draw can be claimed. 75 moves: automatic draw, unless the last move is checkmate. Online platforms use their own implementations.
R0.5 (Law). Flag-fall. Run out of time and you lose — unless your opponent has no possible way to checkmate you; then it is a draw.
R0.6 (Law). Promotion. A pawn reaching the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour. The choice is free.
R0.12 (Principle). The stalemate check. In a winning position, before every move ask: "After my move, does my opponent still have a legal move?"
C0.6 (Concept). Stalemate is the defender's friend. A lone king heads for the corner and for "no-move" positions.

debrief.t: Read their last move for a stalemate or repetition idea: did it leave a king with no legal move?
Count the material: can either side still checkmate at all (dead position)? Note the move count since the last capture or pawn move.
Checks, captures and attacks come after one safety question: after my move, does my opponent still have a legal move?
Calculate to the very last position of the line. A winning line that ends in stalemate, repetition or a dead position is a draw.

courses.endgame.title: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end (level 1)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: Every endgame ends with exactly one of two mechanisms: a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition. Everything else is a lever that helps you create, execute or deny one.
courses.endgame.takeaway: No Wincondition, no win: name yours before you plan.
learn: Every endgame ends with exactly one of two mechanisms: a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition. Everything else is a lever that helps you create, execute or deny one.
Wincondition framework, 0.1 Definition.
A Wincondition is a concrete mechanism that ends the game in your favour. The endgame has exactly two:
– Mate Wincondition — any checkmate attack or mating net.
– Passer Wincondition — any passed pawn: a pawn that no enemy pawn can stop on its own file or on the adjacent files. Its final form is promotion, which normally converts into a Mate Wincondition.
Wincondition framework, 0.2 Everything else is a lever.
Material, king activity, piece activity, space, weak pawns, zugzwang and the tempo count do not win by themselves. They are levers: tools to create a Wincondition, execute it, or deny the opponent's.
Wincondition framework, 0.3 The five laws of the framework.
– Law 1 — No Wincondition, no win. If neither side can create a Wincondition, the position is a draw, whatever the material count.

– Law 2 — Material is not a Wincondition. K+B vs K and K+N vs K are dead draws; K+2N vs K cannot force mate. In endings with only a minor piece against pawns, database statistics put the bishop at about 2½ pawns and the knight even lower — partly because the piece cannot win once its own last pawn disappears.

– Law 3 — Guard the last pawn. Playing for a win, keep at least one pawn: it is the raw material of your Passer Wincondition. Defending, trade pawns: every pawn trade deletes a potential Passer Wincondition.
– Law 4 — Count both sides. Your Wincondition only matters relative to your opponent's. Races are decided by tempi.
– Law 5 — Every exchange changes the Wincondition balance. Before trading, ask: does this trade speed up my Wincondition, or kill my opponent's?
R0.7 (Principle). Name the Wincondition before you plan. Every winning plan ends in a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition.
C0.1 (Concept). What is an endgame? Not a fixed move number but a change of priorities: the kings become fighters, and pawns become the main source of Winconditions.

debrief.t: What did their last move change? Did it create, speed up or stop a Wincondition?
Inventory both sides: is there a passed pawn or a mating net for either side? If neither side has one, the position is a draw.
Forcing moves that create or execute a Wincondition: checks, captures that clear the path and pawn pushes that gain time.
Count the moves to promotion or mate for both sides, including checks and captures on the way.

courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: A five-step scan tells you what to do whenever the position changes character, and a four-rung ladder shows how every won endgame is converted.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Scan, then climb: Secure, Improve, Create, Execute.
learn: A five-step scan tells you what to do whenever the position changes character, and a four-rung ladder shows how every won endgame is converted.
Wincondition framework, 0.5 The Endgame Scan.
Run it whenever the position changes character (an exchange, a pawn break, a new passed pawn):
1. Inventory — Which Winconditions exist for both sides: active, potential, none?
2. Tempo — Who executes first? Count moves to promotion or mate, including checks, captures and queening with check.
3. Levers — Which lever speeds up mine or slows down theirs?
4. Transition test — Can I trade into a known win? Can my opponent trade into a known draw?
5. Decision — Create · Execute · Deny · or Improve ("do not hurry").
Wincondition framework, 0.6 The Conversion Ladder.
Every won endgame is won in this order:
1. Secure — kill counterplay, protect loose pieces and pawns.
2. Improve — centralise the king, activate the worst piece, fix enemy weaknesses.
3. Create — produce a Passer Wincondition or a Mate Wincondition.
4. Execute — escort the Passer Wincondition or deliver mate, without allowing stalemate or perpetual check.

debrief.t: Run the scan after every exchange: what Wincondition did their last move create or deny?
Inventory both sides' Winconditions (active, potential, none) and list the levers: king, rook, space, weak pawns.
Use levers to create or speed up your Wincondition: forcing moves first, quiet improving moves after.
Tempo count and transition test: can I trade into a known win, can they trade into a known draw? Then decide: create, execute, deny or improve.

courses.endgame.title: Wincondition denial: the defender's mirror (level 3)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: The defender has seven ways to deny a Wincondition: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual check and a counter-Wincondition.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Name the denial method before you choose a defence.
learn: The defender has seven ways to deny a Wincondition: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual check and a counter-Wincondition.
Wincondition framework, 0.4 The defender's mirror — Wincondition denial.
1. Blockade — stop the Passer Wincondition on the square directly in front of it (king or knight ideal).
2. Elimination — trade the last pawns; give a piece for the last pawn when the remaining material cannot mate.
3. Theoretical draw — steer into a known drawn position (Philidor, wrong bishop, rook vs bishop).
4. Fortress — a setup the attacker cannot break.
5. Stalemate.
6. Perpetual check or repetition.
7. Counter-Wincondition — create your own Passer or Mate Wincondition so the attacker must stop and defend.

debrief.t: What Wincondition is the opponent building? Name it before you choose a defence.
Which of the seven denial methods exists here: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual or counter-Wincondition?
Blockade or capture first; forcing counterplay (checks, a counter-passer) comes second.
Verify that the denial really holds: calculate the attacker's best breakthrough and every stalemate or repetition resource.
