courses.endgame.title: The Wincondition switch (level 5)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a passer drags defenders to passive squares, then a mating threat strikes the stripped king, or the reverse.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Alternate Passer and Mate Winconditions, and spend the passer when it is worth more as a decoy.
learn: The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a passer drags defenders to passive squares, then a mating threat strikes the stripped king, or the reverse.
C3B.1 (Concept). Advantage transformation — material ↔ activity ↔ structure ↔ Winconditions.

R3C.9 (Principle). The switch. The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a Passer Wincondition that drags defenders to passive squares, then a Mate Wincondition against the stripped king — or mating threats that force the defender to let a passed pawn through.

R3C.10 (Principle). Spend the Passer Wincondition at the right moment. It can be worth more as a decoy than as a queen: its sacrifice deflects a defender, opens a line, or gains the decisive king tempo.

R3C.11 (Principle). Defend with a counter-Wincondition. At the top level the best defence is often a race, not a blockade: create your own Passer or Mate Wincondition and make the attacker spend tempi.
C3C.3 (Concept). The Wincondition switch — alternating Passer and Mate Winconditions until one defence cracks.

debrief.t: Which Wincondition did their last move switch to?
Does a passer drag defenders to passive squares, or does a mating threat force a passed pawn through?
The switch: alternate Passer and Mate Winconditions until one defence cracks; spend the passer as a decoy at the right moment.

courses.endgame.title: Basic mates: queen, rook and the ladder (level 1)
courses.endgame.idea: The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Shrink the box, bring your king, check last, and always ask whether the lone king still has a legal move.
learn: The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
R0.11 (Theory). In the basic mates (K+Q, K+R, K+2B, K+B+N vs K) the lone king is always mated on the edge. Drive it there.
C0.2 (Concept). The edge is a prison. Mate Wincondition technique means shrinking the enemy king's space (the "box") until it stands on the edge.
C0.3 (Concept). The basic mates — your first Mate Wincondition drills.
– K+Q vs K — shrink the box with the queen a knight's move away from the enemy king; when it reaches the edge, stop and bring your own king; mate with king support. At most 10 moves with best play.
– K+R vs K — the rook cuts the board, the king approaches; when the kings face each other, check from the side to push the enemy king back; use rook waiting moves. At most 16 moves.
– K+2R (or K+Q+R) vs K — the ladder: the heavy pieces alternate checks rank by rank. If the king attacks one of them, move it to the far end of its rank.
P0.1 (Must-know position). The stalemate trap. FEN: k7/8/1Q6/8/8/8/8/2K5 b - - 0 1.
Black to move: stalemate. The queen, a knight's move from the cornered king, takes every square but gives no check.

debrief.t: Where did the lone king step? Every king move changes the size of the box you are shrinking.
Locate the edge and the nearest corner, and where your king stands relative to theirs.
Shrink the box with the queen a knight's move away; give a check only when it takes squares away or mates.
Before every move verify stalemate, then count the moves left to mate.

courses.endgame.idea: Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.
courses.endgame.takeaway: B+N: drive the king to the corner of the bishop's colour; 2N cannot mate, but 2N beat a pawn on or behind the Troitzky line.
learn: Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.
R3A.16 (Theory). K+B+N vs K is a forced mate in at most 33 moves: drive the king to a corner of the bishop's colour. Learn the knight's W-manoeuvre (or Delétang's triangle method).
R3A.17 (Theory). K+2B vs K is mate in at most 19 moves. Side-by-side bishops build a wall, the king approaches, and mate can be given in any corner.

R3A.18 (Theory). K+2N vs K cannot be forced — but K+2N vs K+P often can. The knights generally win when the pawn is securely blockaded by a knight on or behind the Troitzky line — Black pawns: a4, b6, c5, d4, e4, f5, g6, h4 (White pawns, mirrored: a5, b3, c4, d5, e5, f4, g3, h5). Some of these wins take more than 50 moves.

debrief.t: Which corner did the lone king head for? With bishop and knight the corner colour matters.
The bishop's colour, the knights' squares and the Troitzky line for the pawn.
Drive the king to the right corner and keep the pieces coordinated; check only when it restricts.

courses.endgame.title: Core principles, typical errors and vocabulary (level 1)
courses.endgame.idea: Once the queens are off the king becomes a fighting piece. These principles, the common errors and the vocabulary carry through every later level.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Activate the king, ahead trade pieces, behind trade pawns, and speak the endgame vocabulary.
learn: Once the queens are off the king becomes a fighting piece. These principles, the common errors and the vocabulary carry through every later level.
R0.8 (Principle). Activate the king. Once the queens are gone, the king is a fighting piece. March it to the centre.
R0.9 (Principle). Know the values. Pawn 1 · knight 3 · bishop 3 · rook 5 · queen 9. An active endgame king fights roughly like a minor piece.
R0.10 (Principle). Ahead → trade pieces, not pawns. Behind → trade pawns, not pieces. (Framework Law 3.)
C0.4 (Concept). Kings move diagonally as fast as straight. A diagonal path is often the shortest route — the seed of the Réti manoeuvre (Tier 2).
Typical errors at Tier 0:
– Stalemating with the queen a knight's move from the cornered king.
– Chasing the king with random checks instead of building the box.
– Leaving the king at home once the queens are off.
– Trading the last pawn while ahead in material.
– Pushing an unsupported pawn straight into the enemy king.
Upgrade triggers: move up when you can do these.
– You mate with K+Q vs K and K+R vs K against a computer from random positions, ten times in a row, without stalemate.
– You apply the rule of the square in seconds, including the double-step case.
– You can list every dead-position material combination.
– You can point out both Winconditions in your own games.
Glossary of endgame vocabulary:

Wincondition — a concrete mechanism that ends the game in your favour: the Mate Wincondition or the Passer Wincondition. · Mate Wincondition — any checkmate attack or mating net. · Passer Wincondition — any passed pawn heading for promotion. · Lever — an advantage that is not itself a Wincondition: material, activity, space, weaknesses, zugzwang. · Candidate — a pawn that can become a passed pawn. · Outside passer — a passed pawn far from the other pawns and the kings. · Protected passer — a passed pawn defended by a pawn. · Opposition — kings facing each other with an odd number of squares between them; the side not to move has it. · Key squares — squares that win for the attacking king, whoever is to move.

Corresponding squares — matching pairs of squares for the two kings. · Mined squares — mutual-zugzwang squares; whoever steps on them first loses. · Triangulation — losing a tempo with a three-square king route. · Zugzwang — having to move is a disadvantage; mutual when it applies to both sides. · Shouldering — blocking the enemy king's path with your own king. · Breakthrough — a pawn sacrifice that creates a passed pawn by force. · Blockade — a piece stopping a passed pawn on the square in front of it. · Fortress — a defensive setup the attacker cannot break. · Cut-off — a rook separating the enemy king from the action along a rank or file.

Short side / long side — the side of a pawn with fewer / more files. · Checking distance — the room a rook needs to check effectively from the flank. · Bridge — Lucena's rook block that ends the checks. · Cross-check — blocking a check with a check. · Domination — taking away every square from an enemy piece. · Dead position — a position in which no series of legal moves can produce checkmate for either side. · WDL / DTZ / DTM — tablebase metrics: win-draw-loss; distance to the next capture or pawn move; distance to mate.

debrief.t: Which piece did the opponent just activate or trade? That tells you whose king and pawns matter now.
King activity, pawn structure and material: ahead you trade pieces, behind you trade pawns.
Activate the king first; checks, captures and attacks come after your king reaches the centre.
Calculate the plan to the end: where does each king stand when the pawn moves arrive?

courses.endgame.title: The rule of the square and your first passed pawns (level 1)
courses.endgame.topic: The rule of the square and first passed pawns
courses.endgame.idea: A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Draw the square before you move: inside it the king catches the pawn, outside it the pawn runs.
learn: A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.

R0.13 (Theory). Rule of the square — stopping a Passer Wincondition with the king. Draw a square from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the defending king is inside it, or steps into it with the move, it catches the pawn (provided nothing blocks its path). A pawn on its starting square counts from one square further, because of the double step.
R0.14 (Principle). King in front, pawn behind. In K+P vs K, lead with the king; the pawn follows.
R0.15 (Theory). The rook pawn is special. K + rook pawn vs K is a draw once the defending king reaches the corner in front of the pawn.
R0.16 (Principle). Push your Passer Wincondition when it is safe. Every step forward ties down more enemy force.
R0.17 (Principle). Blockade enemy Passer Winconditions on the square directly in front of them.

C0.5 (Concept). Passer Wincondition vocabulary. Passed pawn · protected passer (defended by a pawn) · connected passers (adjacent files) · outside passer (far from the other pawns) · candidate (a pawn that can become a passer).
P0.2 (Must-know position). The square. FEN: 7k/8/8/8/1p3K2/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
White to move: 1.Ke3 enters the square and catches the pawn — draw. Black to move: 1...b3 and the Passer Wincondition promotes.
P0.3 (Must-know position). King first. FEN: 8/8/4k3/8/4K3/8/4P3/8 w - - 0 1.
White wins with either side to move: the king is already ahead of its pawn, and the e-pawn's spare moves win the opposition battle (Tier 1).
P0.4 (Must-know position). The rook-pawn corner. FEN: k7/8/1K6/P7/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw with either side to move: the defending king owns the corner.

debrief.t: Which pawn just moved? A pawn push changes the square, so redraw it.
Pawn file and rank, promotion square, both kings; rook pawns are special.
Check whether the defending king is inside the square, or can step into it with the move.
Count the moves for the pawn and for the king; do not forget the double step from the starting square.

courses.endgame.title: Opposition and key squares (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Ask where your king must stand, not which pawn move to play.
learn: Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.

R1.1 (Theory). Opposition. Kings on the same file, rank or diagonal with one square between them: the side not to move has the opposition. With three or five squares between them it is distant opposition — same logic.
R1.2 (Theory). Key squares decide K+P vs K. If the attacking king reaches a key square and the pawn cannot be captured, it wins — no matter who is to move.
– Pawn on its 2nd–4th rank: the three squares two ranks in front of it.
– Pawn on its 5th–6th rank: the three squares one rank in front and the three squares two ranks in front.
– Rook pawn: only the two squares on the adjacent file that touch the promotion square (White a-pawn: b7 and b8).
R1.3 (Theory). Shortcut. With your pawn on the 4th or 5th rank (not a rook pawn), a king on the 6th rank — on the pawn's file or an adjacent file — always stands on a key square.
R1.4 (Principle). Opposition is the tool; key squares are the goal. Use the opposition to shoulder your way onto a key square.
R1.5 (Principle). Defender: stay in front, retreat straight back. In K vs K+P keep your king in front of the pawn; when pushed, step straight backward so you can retake the opposition.
R1.6 (Theory). Spare pawn moves win the opposition. A pawn that has not advanced far keeps tempo moves in reserve — use them to hand the move to the opponent.

R1.7 (Theory). The rook-pawn trap. Refines R0.15. K + rook pawn vs K is also drawn when the defending king controls the two key squares (b7 and b8 against a White a-pawn) — for example by locking the attacking king in front of its own pawn.
C1.1 (Concept). Zugzwang — the obligation to move becomes a disadvantage. It is the engine of every pawn ending.
C1.2 (Concept). The opposition family — direct, distant and diagonal: one parity idea at different distances.
C1.3 (Concept). Key squares — ask "where must my king stand?", not "which pawn move?"
C1.4 (Concept). Spare tempi — pawn moves held in reserve are the currency of pawn endings.
P1.1 (Must-know position). Opposition decides. FEN: 4k3/8/3KP3/8/8/8/8/8 b - - 0 1.
Black to move draws: 1...Kd8! 2.e7+ Ke8 3.Ke6 stalemate. White to move wins: 1.e7 Kf7 2.Kd7 and the pawn queens.

debrief.t: Who just moved? Opposition is about who has to move, so re-read the last move and count tempi.
Pawn rank and file, both kings and the key squares; spare pawn moves are tempo reserves.
Use the opposition to shoulder your king onto a key square; do not push the pawn before the king is ahead of it.
Test both move orders, with you to move and with them to move, and check stalemate on the edge.

courses.endgame.idea: Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Count tempi and routes: the diagonal is as short as the straight line.
learn: Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
R2.1 (Theory). Triangulation. If the position is won with the opponent to move, and your king can use three squares while the enemy king has only two useful ones, walk the triangle to lose a tempo.
R2.2 (Theory). A knight cannot lose a tempo. It changes square colour on every move, so it can never return to the same square in an odd number of moves. Kings, bishops, rooks and queens can.
R2.3 (Theory). Distant and diagonal opposition follow the same parity logic — take them early to win the race to the key squares.
R2.4 (Principle). Shouldering. Use your king's body to block the enemy king's route. Often stronger than approaching directly.

R2.5 (Theory). The Réti manoeuvre. A king moving diagonally can chase two goals at once — hunting an enemy Passer Wincondition while supporting its own. Count diagonal routes before you give up a race.
C2.1 (Concept). Tempo economy — pawn endings are arithmetic: moves to promote, spare moves, king steps.
C2.2 (Concept). Two-goal geometry — the diagonal is as short as the straight line (Réti).
P2.2 (Must-know position). Réti. FEN: 7K/8/k1P5/7p/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw: 1.Kg7 h4 2.Kf6 Kb6 (2...h3 3.Ke7 h2 4.c7 — both pawns queen) 3.Ke5! Kxc6 4.Kf4 — one king walk supported the c-pawn and then caught the h-pawn.

debrief.t: Did the opponent's last move waste or keep a tempo?
Triangle squares for your king and theirs, diagonal routes, and the fact that a knight cannot lose a tempo.
Triangulate to hand over the move; use shouldering and diagonal king walks as forcing moves.
Count three-move and two-move routes: the triangle only works when you have three squares and the enemy king only two.

courses.endgame.title: Corresponding squares and mined squares (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.
learn: Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.

R3A.1 (Theory). Corresponding squares. Opposition is a special case of a larger system: every square of the attacking king has a matching square for the defending king. Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.
R3A.2 (Theory). Mined squares (mutual zugzwang). Some squares are mines — whoever steps on them first loses. Approach them only with the move in hand.

debrief.t: Which mined square did their move step on or avoid?
Key squares first, then correspondence backwards: every square of the attacking king has a defending twin.
Take the squares with the move in hand; never step on a mine.
Map the correspondence from the key squares backwards and test it against every king move.

courses.endgame.title: Tempo parity, routes and domination (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Tempo parity is global: count every spare move on the board, think in routes instead of single moves and take every square from a minor piece.
courses.endgame.takeaway: The last spare tempo wins the mutual zugzwang, and a knight cannot lose a tempo.
learn: Tempo parity is global: count every spare move on the board, think in routes instead of single moves and take every square from a minor piece.
R3C.5 (Principle). Think in routes, not moves. King routes that serve two purposes, rook switches with tempo, queen checks that also centralise.
R3C.6 (Principle). Tempo parity is global. In complex endings, count the spare tempi of the whole board — pawn moves, bishop and rook waiting moves. The last spare tempo wins the mutual zugzwang.

R3C.7 (Principle). Design zugzwangs against knights. Refines R2.2. A knight cannot lose a tempo: aim for positions where the opponent's only free piece is a knight, or where every other waiting move is gone.
R3C.8 (Principle). Domination wins minor pieces. Take away every square of a knight or bishop until it is lost or permanently tied down.
C3C.2 (Concept). Global zugzwang — zugzwang as a whole-board resource, not a king-and-pawn trick.

debrief.t: Which spare tempo did their last move spend?
Global tempo parity: pawn moves, bishop and rook waiting moves, knight tempo traps.
Route the king and rook with tempo; dominate the knight or bishop until it is lost.
Calculate whether the last spare tempo is yours, remembering that a knight cannot lose one.

courses.endgame.title: Outside, protected and separated passed pawns (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Use the outside passer as a decoy, then count the race to the last tempo.
learn: A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
R1.8 (Principle). The outside Passer Wincondition wins pawn endings. Use it as a decoy: while the enemy king runs to stop it, your king invades on the other wing.
R1.9 (Theory). A protected Passer Wincondition cannot be captured by the king alone. As long as its protector stands, the enemy king stays tied to it.
R1.10 (Principle). Separated Passer Winconditions overload a lone king. Check each one with the rule of the square — often one of them promotes.

R1.11 (Theory). Passer Wincondition races. Count the moves to promotion for both sides. Then check the details: does a queen arrive with check, and can the first queen stop the second (by controlling its promotion square, or by skewering king and new queen)?
C1.5 (Concept). Decoy — an outside Passer Wincondition pulls the enemy king away from the real battlefield.
C1.6 (Concept). Underpromotion — a knight for a check or fork, a rook to avoid stalemate (P2.3).
P1.2 (Must-know position). The outside Passer Wincondition as decoy. FEN: 8/8/3k4/8/P2K2p1/6P1/8/8 w - - 0 1.
White wins: 1.a5 Kc6 2.Ke5 Kb5 3.Kf4 Kxa5 4.Kxg4 — Black's king was dragged to a5 while White's king collected g4.

debrief.t: Which king did their last move pull toward which wing? An outside pawn is a decoy.
Outside, protected, connected or separated passers, and the distance of both kings to each pawn.
Push the passer that drags the enemy king away, then invade on the other wing.
Count the race: who queens first, with check, and does the first queen stop the second?

courses.endgame.title: Breakthroughs, majorities, tempi and rook pawns (level 3)
courses.endgame.idea: Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
courses.endgame.takeaway: The candidate moves first; count spare tempi before the kings reach zugzwang.
learn: Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
R2.6 (Theory). The breakthrough. Three pawns on the 5th facing three on the 7th, kings far away: a pawn sacrifice creates a Passer Wincondition by force.
R2.7 (Principle). The candidate moves first. In a pawn majority, advance the pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it — your future Passer Wincondition. The others support it.
R2.8 (Principle). Healthy majorities create Passer Winconditions; crippled (doubled) majorities often cannot.
R2.9 (Principle). Reserve tempi decide blocked pawn endings. Count spare pawn moves on both sides before the kings reach zugzwang. Doubled pawns can be a hidden source of tempi.
R2.10 (Principle). The more active king usually decides the pawn ending.
R2.11 (Principle). Rook pawns are the most drawish pawns in pawn, bishop and rook endings, and against a queen on the 7th. Against a knight they are the most dangerous.
P2.1 (Must-know position). The breakthrough. FEN: 6k1/ppp5/8/PPP5/8/8/8/6K1 w - - 0 1.
White to move wins: 1.b6! axb6 (1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6) 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 and the a-pawn queens. With Black to move, Black's king arrives in time and the breakthrough fails — count the tempi.
P2.3 (Must-know position). Saavedra. FEN: 8/8/1KP5/3r4/8/8/8/k7 w - - 0 1.
White wins: 1.c7 Rd6+ 2.Kb5 Rd5+ 3.Kb4 Rd4+ 4.Kb3 Rd3+ 5.Kc2 Rd4! 6.c8=R! (6.c8=Q? Rc4+ 7.Qxc4 stalemate) Ra4 7.Kb3 — Rc1 mate and Kxa4 are both threatened.

debrief.t: Which pawn is a candidate now? Their last move may have created a passer for you or for them.
Majorities, doubled pawns, rook pawns, reserve tempi and the distance of the kings.
Sacrifice for a breakthrough when the pawns face each other 3 v 3 and the kings are far; otherwise advance the candidate first.
Count tempi after the breakthrough: does the king arrive in time, and does an underpromotion avoid a stalemate?

R3B.15 (Principle). Majorities matter more as material decreases. With both kings on one wing, a majority on the other wing produces an outside Passer Wincondition.

debrief.t: Which majority did their last move weaken or fix?

Advance when it gains space or ties them down; blockade theirs before it gains momentum.

courses.endgame.title: Lucena and Philidor (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Rooks belong behind passed pawns; Lucena builds the bridge, Philidor waits on the third rank and then checks from behind.
learn: Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
R1.16 (Principle). Rooks belong behind Passer Winconditions — behind your own (the rook pushes) and behind the enemy's (the rook attacks while the enemy rook stays stuck in front). Tarrasch's rule.
R1.17 (Principle). Activity first. An active rook is often worth a pawn. A rook passively guarding a pawn is a bad investment.
R1.18 (Principle). Cut off the enemy king. A king cut off from the Passer Wincondition by your rook is out of the game — the first step of almost every winning rook ending.

R1.19 (Theory). Lucena position — WIN ("building a bridge"). Pawn on the 7th (not a rook pawn), attacking king on the promotion square, defending king cut off from the pawn. Method: check the defending king one file further away, lift your rook to the 4th rank, walk your king out, and block the last check with the rook.

R1.20 (Theory). Philidor position — DRAW ("third-rank defence"). Defending king on the promotion square; defending rook on its own third rank, keeping the attacking king off the 6th. The moment the pawn advances to the 6th, swing the rook to the far end of the board and check from behind: the king has lost its shelter.
R1.21 (Principle). Two connected Passer Winconditions on the 6th rank usually beat a lone rook when both kings are far away — unless the rook can win one of them at once, with tempo.
C1.7 (Concept). Cut-off geometry — ranks and files are walls built by rooks.
C1.8 (Concept). The bridge and the shield — in Lucena the rook shields its own king from checks; in Philidor the rook guards the 6th rank, then checks from behind.
P1.4 (Must-know position). Lucena. FEN: 3K4/3P1k2/8/8/8/8/2r5/4R3 w - - 0 1.
White wins: 1.Rf1+ Kg7 2.Rf4! Rc1 3.Ke7 Re1+ 4.Kd6 Rd1+ 5.Ke6 Re1+ 6.Kd5 Rd1+ 7.Rd4 — the bridge.
P1.5 (Must-know position). Philidor. FEN: 4k3/R7/7r/3KP3/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw: 1.e6 Rh1! 2.Kd6 Rd1+ 3.Ke5 Re1+ — checks from behind, forever.

debrief.t: Did their rook cut your king off, or did the pawn advance to the 6th or 7th rank?
Pawn on the 7th, both kings, the cut-off file and where the rooks stand relative to the pawn.
Checks first: in Lucena check from the side and lift the rook to build the bridge, in Philidor wait on the third rank.
Verify every check from a distance and every bridge move: one skipped check ends the win.

courses.endgame.title: The practical rook ending (level 3)
courses.endgame.idea: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Down a pawn, activate before you defend; check from a distance of at least three files.
learn: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
R2.12 (Principle). The rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns from the side and cages the enemy king on the back rank.
R2.13 (Principle). Down a pawn? Activate before you defend. Give a second pawn if needed to activate rook and king. Passive defence usually loses slowly.
R2.14 (Theory). Short side, long side. The defending king goes to the short side of the pawn (fewer files); the defending rook goes to the long side to check from the flank.

R2.15 (Theory). Checking distance. Flank checks normally need three empty files between the checking rook and the pawn (sometimes two with the pawn on the 7th). Any closer, and the attacking king simply walks up to the rook.

R2.16 (Theory). Passive back-rank defence holds only against knight and rook pawns. Refines R1.20. Against bishop and centre pawns it loses once the attacking king reaches the 6th rank on the short side of its pawn: the pawn shields the king from flank checks and the back rank collapses. Use Philidor's defence while you still can.
R2.17 (Principle). 3 vs 2 and 4 vs 3 on the same wing are usually drawn in rook endings. An extra pawn wins far more often when it is a distant Passer Wincondition.
R2.18 (Principle). "All rook endings are drawn." Tartakower's quip is a warning, not a law. Rook endings are the most common endgame type and among the most drawish: a pawn up is not yet a win.
C2.3 (Concept). Activity as material — an active rook or king often outweighs a pawn.
C2.7 (Concept). The Mate Wincondition in rook endings — a king cut off on the back rank, plus an active rook and king, can produce mating nets even with many pawns left.

debrief.t: Did their rook go passive? Down a pawn: activate; a pawn up: ask what they now threaten.
Rook on the 7th, short side versus long side of the pawn, checking distance, centre pawn versus rook pawn.
Checks and rook activity first: flank checks from at least three files away.
Verify the checking distance, then count whether passive defence holds against bishop and centre pawns.

courses.endgame.title: The rook canon: Rule of Five, Vančura and the g7/h7 rule (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Rook behind the pawn, flank checks from distance, and the defending king on g7 or h7 against a rook pawn.
learn: The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.

R3A.5 (Principle). The Rule of Five. Pawn protected, defending king cut off by files: add the pawn's rank to the number of files the defending king is cut off. More than five: usually a win. Five or less: normally a draw. Knight and rook pawns are exceptions.
R3A.6 (Theory). Against a pawn on the 7th, only flank checks work; against a pawn on the 6th, checks from behind work too — the Philidor mechanism.

R3A.7 (Theory). Vančura position — DRAW. Rook pawn on the 6th with the attacking rook in front of it: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the side along the 6th rank, and the defending king shuttles between g7 and h7 (against an a-pawn). Meet the approaching king with checks from the side, keeping your distance; if the pawn advances to the 7th, put the rook behind it (R3A.8).

R3A.8 (Theory). The g7/h7 rule. Rook pawn on the 7th, attacking rook in front (Ra8, Pa7), defending rook behind the pawn: a draw with the defending king on g7 or h7. Anywhere else, a rook check or skewer usually forces the pawn through (e.g., Rh8! Rxa7, Rh7+).

R3A.9 (Principle). Rook + two pawns vs rook usually wins — connected pawns most easily. The notorious exception is f- and h-pawns: often a theoretical draw with an excellent defence, yet regularly lost in practice.

R3A.10 (Principle). Rook vs connected Passer Winconditions. Refines R1.21. The rook attacks from behind and the rook side's king must come fast; the pawns win when they reach the 6th with tempo and the rook cannot pick one of them off.
P3A.1 (Must-know position). Vančura. FEN: R7/6k1/P4r2/8/2K5/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.

Draw: Black's rook stays on the 6th, hitting a6 from the side; the king shuttles g7–h7; an approaching White king is met by checks from the side. If 1.a7, then 1...Ra6 — rook behind the pawn, king on g7.
P3A.3 (Must-know position). The g7/h7 rule.
R7/P5k1/8/8/8/8/r7/6K1 w - - 0 1 — Draw: the king stands on g7.
R7/P4k2/8/8/8/8/r7/6K1 w - - 0 1 — White wins: 1.Rh8! (1...Rxa7 2.Rh7+ and 3.Rxa7).

debrief.t: Which rook position did their last move aim for: Philidor, Vančura or g7/h7?

R3B.21 (Principle). In rook endings, counterplay beats passive material defence. The side that creates a Passer Wincondition first often wins even while behind in pawns.

courses.endgame.title: Queen endings: winning zone, fortresses and cross-checks (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Use cross-checks against perpetual, and never capture the pawn when it is stalemate.
learn: The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.

R3A.11 (Theory). The winning zone. Refines R1.13. Against bishop and rook pawns on the 7th, the queen still wins when the attacking king is close enough to create a Mate Wincondition or to support the capture.

R3A.12 (Theory). Queen vs rook is a win (barring immediate tactics). Drive the king to the edge, then separate rook and king by zugzwang — the queen can pass the move with a triangle of checks (P3A.4) — and finish with a fork or mate.
R3A.13 (Theory). Queen vs rook + pawn can be a fortress. A rook on its third rank, protected by a pawn on its second rank next to its king, often cannot be broken.
R3A.14 (Principle). In queen endings the Passer Wincondition outranks material. A far-advanced passer escorted by the queen beats one or two extra pawns elsewhere.

R3A.15 (Principle). Perpetual check is the defender's main denial tool. The attacker centralises the queen, uses pawns as shelter, and answers checks with cross-checks — blocking a check while giving check.
C3A.5 (Concept). Cross-check — blocking a check with a check; the attacker's weapon against perpetual.
P3A.2 (Must-know position). Queen vs bishop pawn. FEN: 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/1kp5/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw: 1.Qb6+ Ka1! 2.Qd4+ Kb1 3.Qb4+ Ka1 4.Qc3+ Kb1 5.Qb3+ Ka1! — 6.Qxc2 is stalemate, and White's king is too far away to help.
Contrast (same setup): the centre pawn 7K/8/7Q/8/8/8/2kp4/8 w - - 0 1 and the knight pawn 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/kp6/8 w - - 0 1 are White wins; the rook pawn 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/pk6/8 w - - 0 1 is a draw.
P3A.4 (Must-know position). Queen vs rook: the zugzwang triangle. FEN: 1k6/1r6/2K5/Q7/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
White wins. With Black to move this is zugzwang: the rook must leave its king. With White to move, pass the move: 1.Qe5+ Ka8 2.Qa1+ Kb8 3.Qa5 — same position, Black to move.

R2.19 (Principle). Good bishop, bad bishop. A bishop is bad when its own pawns are fixed on its colour. Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop; fix enemy pawns on the colour of your bishop so you can attack them.
R2.20 (Principle). Bishop vs knight. Bishops prefer open positions and pawns on both wings; knights prefer closed positions, outposts and all pawns on one wing.
R2.21 (Principle). Knight endings behave like pawn endings (Botvinnik). The outside Passer Wincondition and king activity are even more decisive than usual.
R2.25 (Principle). Blockade with the right piece. The knight is the ideal blockader of a Passer Wincondition — it stays active on the blockade square. In endings, so is the king.
C2.4 (Concept). Colour complexes — a bishop fights for one colour; pawns and the king must cover the other.
C2.5 (Concept). Blockade — the main Wincondition-denial tool in minor-piece endings.

learn: One weakness can be defended, two cannot. When the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first.

R2.27 (Principle). Do not hurry. If the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first. The decisive break comes when everything is ready.
R2.28 (Principle). The pawn-ending test. Before trading into a pawn ending, remove all pieces in your head and ask who wins. Winning → trade. Not winning → keep pieces.

– Attacking one weakness forever instead of creating a second.

courses.endgame.title: Fortresses, stalemate architecture and the 50-move horizon (Tier 3A checklist) (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: A fortress is a setup the attacker cannot break; stalemate can be a designed defence; theory and the 50-move rule can disagree.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Before simplifying, ask whether the defender can build a setup you cannot break.
learn: A fortress is a setup the attacker cannot break; stalemate can be a designed defence; theory and the 50-move rule can disagree.
C3A.3 (Concept). Fortress (introduction) — a static setup the attacker cannot break: wrong bishop, opposite-bishop blockade, queen vs rook + pawn.
C3A.4 (Concept). Stalemate architecture — stalemate as a designed defence: queen vs c/f/a/h pawns, desperado rooks, the wrong-bishop corner.
C3A.6 (Concept). The 50-move horizon — several theoretical wins (2B vs N, 2N vs P, Q vs 2B) collide with the 50-move rule. Theory and practice can give different results.
Appendix A, theoretical results at a glance:
"Generally" means exceptions exist in specific positions. Move counts assume best play.
Mate Wincondition — the basic mates:
– K+Q vs K — win, at most 10 moves
– K+R vs K — win, at most 16 moves
– K+2B vs K (opposite colours) — win, at most 19 moves
– K+B+N vs K — win, at most 33 moves
– K+2N vs K — no forced mate
– K+B vs K · K+N vs K — dead position
Pawnless endings:
– Q vs R — generally a win
– Q vs 2B — generally a win (up to 71 moves)
– Q vs 2N — many wins, but a large share of draws
– R vs B — generally a draw (defending king to the corner not of its bishop's colour)
– R vs N — generally a draw (knight next to its king, away from corners)
– R+B vs R — generally a draw (Philidor and Lolli positions win; Cochrane and second-rank defences hold)
– R+N vs R — generally a draw
– 2B vs N — generally a win (some wins exceed 50 moves)
Passer Wincondition endings:
– K+P vs K — decided by key squares
– K + rook pawn vs K — draw once the defender reaches the corner or traps the attacking king
– K+B + wrong rook pawn vs K — draw once the defending king reaches the corner
– Q vs pawn on the 7th — win vs b/d/e/g pawns; vs a/c/f/h pawns a draw unless the attacking king is close
– R+P vs R — Lucena wins; Philidor and Vančura draw; the Rule of Five as a guide
– R+2P vs R — usually a win (f+h notoriously drawish)
– 2N vs P — generally a win when blockaded on or behind the Troitzky line (sometimes beyond 50 moves)
– Q vs R+P — fortress draws exist
– Opposite-coloured bishops — +1 usually drawn; +2 depends on the distance between the passed pawns
Typical errors at Tier 3A:
– Assuming every rook-pawn ending is drawn — the defending king must reach g7/h7 (R3A.8).
– Starting flank checks too close to the pawn (R2.15).
– B+N mate: pushing the king to the wrong corner and never switching.
– Taking the bishop pawn with the queen when it is stalemate (P3A.2).
– Allowing a queen vs rook + pawn fortress when pieces could have been kept.
– Forgetting the 50-move count in 2B vs N, 2N vs P and Q vs 2B.
Upgrade triggers: move up when you can do these.
– You mate with K+B+N vs K well inside 50 moves under blitz conditions.
– You win Lucena and hold Philidor and Vančura against an engine from random starts.
– You recite the Troitzky line and the queen-vs-pawn rule without notes.
– You survive 50 moves of R vs R+B against an engine with the Cochrane defence.

debrief.t: Is the defender heading for a fortress or a stalemate setup?
Static versus dynamic fortresses: wrong bishop, opposite bishops, queen versus rook plus pawn.
Before simplifying, ask: can the defender build a setup I cannot break?
Count the 50-move horizon: theory and practice can differ.

courses.endgame.title: The art of exchanging (Tier 3B checklist) (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Trade the defender's best piece, keep your best attacker, convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage and know what each exchange does.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Name what the exchange does before you make it.
learn: Trade the defender's best piece, keep your best attacker, convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage and know what each exchange does.
R3B.5 (Principle). Trade the defender's best piece; keep your best attacker.

R3B.6 (Principle). Convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage. An extra pawn converts most reliably in pawn and minor-piece endings (except opposite-coloured bishops), least reliably in rook and opposite-bishop endings. See Appendix B.

R3B.7 (Principle). Know what each exchange does. It removes a defender against your Passer Wincondition, removes an attacker from the opponent's Mate Wincondition, or changes the endgame type. Name which one before you trade.
R3B.8 (Principle). The defender trades pawns and chooses the drawing material — rook endings, opposite-coloured bishops, the wrong bishop, the queen vs rook + pawn fortress.
Appendix B, the extra pawn: conversion ladder (principle). From easiest to hardest in typical positions; structure and activity can overturn the order:
– Pawn endings — usually winning.
– Knight endings — usually winning.
– Same-coloured bishop endings — often winning; harder if your pawns sit on your bishop's colour.
– Queen endings — real winning chances, but perpetual check is always lurking.
– Rook endings — often drawn.
– Opposite-coloured bishop endings — usually drawn.
Typical errors at Tier 3B:
– Trading pieces automatically when ahead — straight into a rook or opposite-bishop ending.
– Pushing pawns into the defender's zone before the king is ready (hurrying).
– Activating the king while enemy heavy pieces can still build a Mate Wincondition.
– Defending one weakness passively instead of creating counterplay.
– Planning without asking what the opponent wants.
Upgrade triggers: move up when you can do these.
– In your own games you can name the exchange that changed the Wincondition balance, and why.
– You convert slightly better endings with no extra material against strong opposition.
– You annotate a master endgame without an engine, and your plans match the engine's key decisions.

debrief.t: Which defender did their last move bring in, and can I trade it?
Which endgame type magnifies my advantage: pawn and minor-piece endings versus rook and opposite-bishop endings.
Trade the defender's best piece; keep your best attacker; name what the exchange does.
Test the resulting ending (pawn-ending test, fortress test) before you trade.

courses.endgame.title: Planning, prophylaxis and the king (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Picture the ideal setup first, ask what the opponent wants, improve your worst piece and restrict before you attack.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Prophylaxis first, then restrict, then attack, and calculate only where the opponent can interfere.
learn: Picture the ideal setup first, ask what the opponent wants, improve your worst piece and restrict before you attack.
R3B.1 (Principle). Schematic thinking. Before calculating, picture the ideal setup — where every piece and the king belong — and the route there. Calculate only where the opponent can interfere.
R3B.2 (Principle). Prophylaxis first. Ask what your opponent wants: usually an active rook, a Passer Wincondition or a known draw. Stop that before pursuing your own plan.
R3B.3 (Principle). Improve the worst piece. In slow endings, the side whose worst piece is better usually wins.
R3B.4 (Principle). Restrict before you attack. Take squares away from the enemy king and pieces first; Winconditions become unstoppable once the defender is paralysed.

R3B.18 (Principle). The king-safety paradox. With queens or two rooks each on the board, activity and safety compete: the Mate Wincondition is still alive. Activate the king only where enemy heavy pieces cannot build a mating net.
R3B.19 (Principle). Pawns are an umbrella. A king beside or in front of its pawns is shielded from checks along those lines.
R3B.26 (Principle). Clock economy. In long endings play the obvious improving moves quickly; spend your time at transitions — exchanges, pawn breaks, entering theoretical positions.
R3B.27 (Law). Count the 50 moves yourself in long defences (R+B vs R, Q vs 2B): every capture or pawn move resets the count.
C3B.2 (Concept). Domination — controlling every square an enemy piece could use.
C3B.3 (Concept). Two weaknesses, deep version — the second weakness can be a Mate Wincondition threat rather than a pawn.
C3B.4 (Concept). Harmony — pieces protecting each other and the king, so that no tactic interrupts the plan.

debrief.t: What does the opponent want: an active rook, a passer or a known draw?
The ideal setup for every piece, the worst piece, and the king-safety paradox.

courses.endgame.title: Transformations and structure-born endgames (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Turn a static advantage into a dynamic one at the right moment, and know which endgames your middlegame structures leave behind.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Return material or sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition.
learn: Turn a static advantage into a dynamic one at the right moment, and know which endgames your middlegame structures leave behind.
R3B.11 (Principle). Turn static advantages into dynamic ones at the right moment — return material to activate your king or rook, or to create an unstoppable Passer Wincondition.

R3B.12 (Principle). Sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition. Two threats — a Passer Wincondition on one wing, a king invasion or Mate Wincondition on the other — break defences that hold against one.
R3B.14 (Principle). Structural weaknesses grow as pieces disappear. Isolated, doubled and backward pawns are defended by pieces; every exchange removes a defender.
R3B.16 (Principle). Fix, then attack. Fix enemy pawns on squares your pieces can hit, then bring the king.
R3B.17 (Principle). Create an entry square. Kings win endings by invasion — use a pawn lever to open a door.
C3B.5 (Concept). Structure-born endgames — what middlegame structures leave behind:
– Isolated queen's pawn — its dynamism fades with every exchange; the pawn becomes a target and the square in front of it a permanent blockade post.
– Hanging pawns — dynamic with pieces on the board; targets that need constant protection without them.
– Carlsbad (minority attack) — the minority attack leaves a weak pawn (usually on c6 or c3) that becomes the main endgame target.

– …c6 structures after …dxe4 (Caro-Kann main lines) — White has a 4 vs 3 majority on the queenside (a–d vs a–c), Black on the kingside (e–h vs f–h). With both kings castled short, the queenside majority is the one that produces the outside Passer Wincondition.
– Doubled pawns — a crippled majority may never create a Passer Wincondition, but the extra pawn controls squares and supplies spare tempi.
– Space advantage — worth less as pieces come off; the cramped side usually welcomes exchanges.

debrief.t: Which static advantage does their last move allow me to transform?
Isolated, hanging, Carlsbad, ...c6 structures, doubled pawns and space.
Return material to activate; sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition.
Verify the transformation: material for activity must create an unstoppable threat.

courses.endgame.title: Fortress and anti-fortress (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Test for fortresses before you simplify, know the warning signs and the toolkit for breaking them.
courses.endgame.takeaway: A large engine evaluation with no visible progress is a fortress alarm.
learn: Test for fortresses before you simplify, know the warning signs and the toolkit for breaking them.
R3C.1 (Principle). Test for fortresses before you simplify. At every major exchange ask: "Afterwards, can the defender build a setup I cannot break?" If yes, change the structure first — then trade.

R3C.2 (Principle). Fortress warning signs. The defender has safe waiting moves; your king has no entry square; the blockaders cannot be attacked by enough pieces; your pawns are fixed on the wrong colour.

R3C.3 (Principle). The anti-fortress toolkit. Zugzwang (remove the waiting moves) · pawn breaks and sacrifices that open entry lines · changing the colour complex of the pawns · exchanging the key defender · returning material to reach a known win · a second Wincondition on the other wing.

R3C.4 (Principle). Engines can misjudge fortresses. A large evaluation with no visible progress over long lines is a fortress alarm. Check with tablebases (up to 7 pieces) or search for a concrete break yourself.
C3C.1 (Concept). Static vs dynamic fortresses — static: the attacker has no entry at all; dynamic: the defender holds only with exact waiting moves or perpetual threats.

debrief.t: Did their last move give them a safe waiting move?
Fortress signs: waiting moves, no entry square, blockaders that cannot be attacked, pawns fixed on the wrong colour.
Anti-fortress toolkit: zugzwang, breaks and sacrifices, change the colour complex, exchange the key defender.
Check with tablebases or find a concrete break; engine numbers can mislead.

courses.endgame.title: Grandmaster technique (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Maximum problems for the opponent, minimum risk for you; repeat once, never three times; know tablebase metrics and build a personal anchor library.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Calculate backwards from the anchor and choose methods you can execute inside the 50-move horizon.
learn: Maximum problems for the opponent, minimum risk for you; repeat once, never three times; know tablebase metrics and build a personal anchor library.
R3C.17 (Principle). Maximum problems, minimum risk. In equal or slightly better endings, choose lines that demand accurate moves from the opponent for a long time while you keep zero losing risk.
R3C.18 (Principle). Repeat once to gain time — never three times. A single repetition banks clock time and tests whether the defender knows the right waiting moves.

R3C.19 (Law). The flag-fall nuance. Refines R0.5. You lose on time if your opponent could checkmate you by any series of legal moves — even a helpmate. So K+N or K+B against your K+P can still win on time; against your bare king they cannot.

R3C.20 (Principle). Tablebase literacy. Learn WDL (win/draw/loss), DTZ (distance to the next capture or pawn move that resets the 50-move count) and DTM (distance to mate). All positions with up to 7 pieces are solved and partial 8-piece work is ongoing — expect published "rules" to keep being refined.
R3C.21 (Principle). A win beyond 50 moves is not a practical win. Choose winning methods a human can execute inside the 50-move horizon.
R3C.22 (Principle). Know the endgames your openings produce. Every repertoire has typical structures; steer the middlegame toward endings where your structure's Winconditions are healthier.
R3C.23 (Principle). Calculate backwards from the anchor. Identify the target theoretical position first, then find the move order that reaches it with the right side to move.
R3C.24 (Principle). Build a personal anchor library — 100–150 positions you can play perfectly from both sides, grouped by material and structure, reviewed with spaced repetition.
C3C.4 (Concept). Practical probability — choosing lines by how hard they are for the opponent, not only by their evaluation.

C3C.5 (Concept). Model technique — Capablanca (simplification), Rubinstein (rook endings), Smyslov (harmony), Karpov (restriction and domination), Fischer (bishop vs knight), Carlsen (pressure in equal endings).
Typical errors at Tier 3C:
– Simplifying straight into a fortress.
– Trusting engine numbers in blocked positions.
– Winning too slowly and running into the 50-move rule.
– Applying theory without its exceptions: knight pawns in the Rule of Five, the wrong rook pawn in opposite-bishop endings, the king's square in rook-pawn endings.
Grandmaster standard:
– You explain any endgame result through its Winconditions and denial mechanisms.
– You steer ten to twenty moves ahead into anchor positions.
– You win "equal" endings against masters and hold worse ones against stronger players.

debrief.t: Which line gives the opponent the most problems while I risk nothing?
Your anchor library, practical probability and the 50-move horizon.
Maximum problems, minimum risk; repeat once, never three times.
Calculate backwards from the anchor; choose methods executable within 50 moves.

egtabs.label: Free / Foundations
egtabs.tagline: Know what wins, what draws, and how to finish.

tiers.name: Tier 0 · Foundations
tiers.mission: know what wins, what draws, and how to finish.
errors: Stalemating with the queen a knight's move from the cornered king.
Chasing the king with random checks instead of building the box.
Leaving the king at home once the queens are off.
Trading the last pawn while ahead in material.
Pushing an unsupported pawn straight into the enemy king.
triggers: You mate with K+Q vs K and K+R vs K against a computer from random positions, ten times in a row, without stalemate.
You apply the rule of the square in seconds, including the double-step case.
You can list every dead-position material combination.
You can point out both Winconditions in your own games.

egtabs.splitRule: Anchor = the Learn puzzle. The other puzzles of a theme are ordered by difficulty = rating + 4 x pieces + 8 x solver moves (tier midpoint for the hand-built Blueprint positions). Easier half = simple puzzles, harder half = hard puzzles.

egtabs.label: Beginner / Speedcourse
egtabs.tagline: King-and-pawn endings and the first rook positions.

tiers.name: Tier 1 · Speedcourse
tiers.mission: master king-and-pawn endings and meet the first theoretical rook positions.
errors: Pushing the pawn early and losing the opposition.
Defending K vs K+P from the side instead of in front.
Philidor: dropping the rook to the back rank before the pawn reaches the 6th, letting the attacking king in.
Lucena: skipping the bridge and walking into endless checks.
Queen vs c/f/a/h pawn: capturing the pawn when it gives stalemate.
triggers: You win every won K+P vs K position and hold every drawn one against an engine.
You play Lucena and Philidor from memory — from both sides.
You win five different pawn endings with an outside Passer Wincondition against a computer.
You can explain why the wrong bishop draws.

egtabs.label: Intermediate
egtabs.tagline: Control tempo, value activity, start thinking strategically.

tiers.name: Tier 2 · Intermediate
tiers.mission: control tempo, value activity, and start thinking strategically.
errors: Entering a rook ending a pawn up and treating it as won (R2.18).
Waiting passively on the back rank against a centre pawn (R2.16).
Checking from the flank with the rook too close to the pawn (R2.15).
Fixing your own pawns on your bishop's colour.
Trading the last rooks without the pawn-ending test (R2.28).
Attacking one weakness forever instead of creating a second.
triggers: You solve triangulation and breakthrough exercises by visualisation only.
You hold a rook ending a pawn down through activity against a stronger opponent or an engine.
You win a bishop-vs-knight ending with pawns on both wings.
You can explain why opposite-coloured bishops are drawish on their own and dangerous with rooks.

egtabs.label: Advanced
egtabs.tagline: The theoretical anchor positions, known cold.

tiers.name: Tier 3A · Theoretical Endgames
tiers.mission: know the anchor positions cold — the targets you steer toward or away from.
errors: Assuming every rook-pawn ending is drawn — the defending king must reach g7/h7 (R3A.8).
Starting flank checks too close to the pawn (R2.15).
B+N mate: pushing the king to the wrong corner and never switching.
Taking the bishop pawn with the queen when it is stalemate (P3A.2).
Allowing a queen vs rook + pawn fortress when pieces could have been kept.
Forgetting the 50-move count in 2B vs N, 2N vs P and Q vs 2B.
triggers: You mate with K+B+N vs K well inside 50 moves under blitz conditions.
You win Lucena and hold Philidor and Vančura against an engine from random starts.
You recite the Troitzky line and the queen-vs-pawn rule without notes.
You survive 50 moves of R vs R+B against an engine with the Cochrane defence.

egtabs.label: Master / Grandmaster
egtabs.tagline: Plans, exchanges, fortresses and grandmaster technique.

tiers.name: Tier 3B · Endgame Strategy
tiers.mission: think like a master — plans, exchanges and transformations instead of isolated positions.
errors: Trading pieces automatically when ahead — straight into a rook or opposite-bishop ending.
Pushing pawns into the defender's zone before the king is ready (hurrying).
Activating the king while enemy heavy pieces can still build a Mate Wincondition.
Defending one weakness passively instead of creating counterplay.
Planning without asking what the opponent wants.
triggers: In your own games you can name the exchange that changed the Wincondition balance, and why.
You convert slightly better endings with no extra material against strong opposition.
You annotate a master endgame without an engine, and your plans match the engine's key decisions.

tiers.name: Tier 3C · Grandmaster Deep Dives
tiers.mission: the invisible layer — fortresses, geometry, maximal technique and practical dominance.
errors: Simplifying straight into a fortress.
Trusting engine numbers in blocked positions.
Winning too slowly and running into the 50-move rule.
Applying theory without its exceptions: knight pawns in the Rule of Five, the wrong rook pawn in opposite-bishop endings, the king's square in rook-pawn endings.
triggers: You explain any endgame result through its Winconditions and denial mechanisms.
You steer ten to twenty moves ahead into anchor positions.
You win "equal" endings against masters and hold worse ones against stronger players.

egthemes.title: The laws that decide endgames (level 1)
egthemes.idea: Before technique, know when a game is already over: stalemate, dead position, repetition, the 50-move rule, flag-fall and the free choice of promotion piece.
egthemes.takeaway: A won position is only won if you do not stalemate, repeat or run out of time.

egthemes.title: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end (level 1)
egthemes.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
egthemes.idea: Every endgame ends with exactly one of two mechanisms: a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition. Everything else is a lever that helps you create, execute or deny one.
egthemes.takeaway: No Wincondition, no win: name yours before you plan.

egthemes.title: Basic mates: queen, rook and the ladder (level 1)
egthemes.idea: The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
egthemes.takeaway: Shrink the box, bring your king, check last, and always ask whether the lone king still has a legal move.

egthemes.title: Core principles, typical errors and vocabulary (level 1)
egthemes.idea: Once the queens are off the king becomes a fighting piece. These principles, the common errors and the vocabulary carry through every later level.
egthemes.takeaway: Activate the king, ahead trade pieces, behind trade pawns, and speak the endgame vocabulary.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: The rule of the square and your first passed pawns (level 1)
egthemes.topic: The rule of the square and first passed pawns
egthemes.idea: A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.
egthemes.takeaway: Draw the square before you move: inside it the king catches the pawn, outside it the pawn runs.

egthemes.title: The Endgame Scan and the Conversion Ladder (level 2)
egthemes.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
egthemes.idea: A five-step scan tells you what to do whenever the position changes character, and a four-rung ladder shows how every won endgame is converted.
egthemes.takeaway: Scan, then climb: Secure, Improve, Create, Execute.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Opposition and key squares (level 2)
egthemes.idea: Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.
egthemes.takeaway: Ask where your king must stand, not which pawn move to play.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Outside, protected and separated passed pawns (level 2)
egthemes.idea: A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
egthemes.takeaway: Use the outside passer as a decoy, then count the race to the last tempo.

egthemes.title: Lucena and Philidor (level 2)
egthemes.idea: Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
egthemes.takeaway: Rooks belong behind passed pawns; Lucena builds the bridge, Philidor waits on the third rank and then checks from behind.

egthemes.title: Queen versus a pawn on the seventh (level 2)
egthemes.idea: A queen usually stops a pawn on the seventh, but against bishop and rook pawns the stalemate tricks save the defender.
egthemes.takeaway: Check and pin until the king steps in front of its pawn, and never capture into a stalemate.

egthemes.title: The wrong bishop and minor pieces against passed pawns (level 2)
egthemes.idea: A bishop with a rook pawn only wins if it controls the promotion square, and minor pieces stop passers in different ways.
egthemes.takeaway: If the bishop does not control the corner, the corner is a fortress.

egthemes.title: Converting an extra pawn (Tier 1 checklist) (level 2)
egthemes.idea: Winning a pawn is step one of three: win it, turn it into a passer, escort it home. Calculate every trade into a pawn ending.
egthemes.takeaway: Win the pawn, make a passer, escort it home, and only trade into pawn endings you have calculated.

egthemes.title: Wincondition denial: the defender's mirror (level 3)
egthemes.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
egthemes.idea: The defender has seven ways to deny a Wincondition: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual check and a counter-Wincondition.
egthemes.takeaway: Name the denial method before you choose a defence.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Triangulation, shouldering and the Réti manoeuvre (level 3)
egthemes.idea: Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
egthemes.takeaway: Count tempi and routes: the diagonal is as short as the straight line.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Breakthroughs, majorities, tempi and rook pawns (level 3)
egthemes.idea: Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
egthemes.takeaway: The candidate moves first; count spare tempi before the kings reach zugzwang.

egthemes.title: The practical rook ending (level 3)
egthemes.idea: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
egthemes.takeaway: Down a pawn, activate before you defend; check from a distance of at least three files.

egthemes.title: Good bishop, bad bishop, bishop versus knight and the blockade (level 3)
egthemes.idea: Pawns on the bishop's colour make it bad; knights love closed positions and blockade squares; knight endings behave like pawn endings.
egthemes.takeaway: Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop and blockade with a knight or the king.

egthemes.title: Opposite-coloured bishops (level 3)
egthemes.idea: Alone, opposite-coloured bishops are drawish even a pawn or two down; with rooks or queens they favour the attacker.
egthemes.takeaway: Bishops only: blockade on your bishop's colour. With heavy pieces: attack the colour their bishop cannot guard.

egthemes.title: Rook versus a minor piece: the corner decides (level 3)
egthemes.topic: Rook versus minor pieces and material balance
egthemes.idea: Without pawns a rook usually cannot beat a minor piece: the defender has to run to the right corner.
egthemes.takeaway: Against a bishop run to the corner not of its colour; against a knight stay next to your knight and avoid corners.

egthemes.title: Two weaknesses, do not hurry and the pawn-ending test (Tier 2 checklist) (level 3)
egthemes.idea: One weakness can be defended, two cannot. When the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first.
egthemes.takeaway: Create a second weakness, do not hurry, and run the pawn-ending test before every trade.

egthemes.title: Anchor positions and zones (level 4)
egthemes.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
egthemes.idea: Theory is a map of targets: steer toward winning anchors and away from drawn ones, and know the zones where the defending king must stand.
egthemes.takeaway: Calculate backwards from the anchor position.

egthemes.title: Advanced mates and the Troitzky line (level 4)
egthemes.idea: Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.
egthemes.takeaway: B+N: drive the king to the corner of the bishop's colour; 2N cannot mate, but 2N beat a pawn on or behind the Troitzky line.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Corresponding squares and mined squares (level 4)
egthemes.idea: Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.
egthemes.takeaway: Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Outside versus protected passers and the queening race (level 4)
egthemes.idea: Calculate, do not quote slogans: compare how long the outside passer distracts the king with how long the protected passer ties it down.
egthemes.takeaway: A queening race is only half the calculation: check what happens after both queens appear.

egthemes.title: The rook canon: Rule of Five, Vančura and the g7/h7 rule (level 4)
egthemes.idea: The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.
egthemes.takeaway: Rook behind the pawn, flank checks from distance, and the defending king on g7 or h7 against a rook pawn.

egthemes.title: Queen endings: winning zone, fortresses and cross-checks (level 4)
egthemes.idea: The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.
egthemes.takeaway: Use cross-checks against perpetual, and never capture the pawn when it is stalemate.

egthemes.title: Knight, bishop and pawn endings (level 4)
egthemes.idea: Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare, bishops need a diagonal across the pawn's path, and a knight can give itself up for the last pawn.
egthemes.takeaway: Control the promotion square or reach it in time; K+N versus K is a dead position.

egthemes.title: Pawnless endings: 2B v N, R+B v R, queen v minor pieces (level 4)
egthemes.topic: Rook versus minor pieces and material balance
egthemes.idea: Tablebases overturned old verdicts: two bishops beat a knight, queen beats two bishops, but the 50-move rule can rescue the defender.
egthemes.takeaway: Know the winning and drawing verdicts, and count the 50 moves yourself.

egthemes.title: Fortresses, stalemate architecture and the 50-move horizon (Tier 3A checklist) (level 4)
egthemes.idea: A fortress is a setup the attacker cannot break; stalemate can be a designed defence; theory and the 50-move rule can disagree.
egthemes.takeaway: Before simplifying, ask whether the defender can build a setup you cannot break.

egthemes.title: The Wincondition switch (level 5)
egthemes.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
egthemes.idea: The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a passer drags defenders to passive squares, then a mating threat strikes the stripped king, or the reverse.
egthemes.takeaway: Alternate Passer and Mate Winconditions, and spend the passer when it is worth more as a decoy.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Tempo parity, routes and domination (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Tempo parity is global: count every spare move on the board, think in routes instead of single moves and take every square from a minor piece.
egthemes.takeaway: The last spare tempo wins the mutual zugzwang, and a knight cannot lose a tempo.

egthemes.chapTitle: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares
egthemes.title: Passed pawns and majorities at master level (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Advance your passers when it gains space or ties the opponent down, blockade theirs early, and use the majority on the wing the kings left.
egthemes.takeaway: With both kings on one wing, the majority on the other wing makes the outside passer.

egthemes.title: The grandmaster layer of rook endings (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Activity can outweigh two pawns: the side that completes its triangle of active rook, active king and passer first usually wins.
egthemes.takeaway: Know the drawing zones exactly, so you can calculate transitions into R+P versus R long before they happen.

egthemes.title: Queen and heavy-piece endings at master level (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Queen endings are races of passers and checks; trust the position rather than the piece myth.
egthemes.takeaway: King safety, colour complexes and passers decide, not slogans.

egthemes.title: Knight versus bad bishop and bishop versus knight (level 5)
egthemes.idea: A knight against a bad bishop generates Winconditions by itself; with pawns on both wings, create a passer on one wing and invade on the other.
egthemes.takeaway: Fix pawns on the bishop's colour, occupy key squares and use zugzwang.

egthemes.title: Opposite-coloured bishops: the winning recipe (level 5)
egthemes.idea: To win with opposite-coloured bishops you need two passers far apart; connected passers must reach the sixth rank.
egthemes.takeaway: One file apart is usually a draw; three or more files normally wins.

egthemes.title: Material by the numbers and up the exchange (level 5)
egthemes.topic: Rook versus minor pieces and material balance
egthemes.idea: Database numbers: bishop and knight are equal on average, the bishop pair is worth about half a pawn, rooks gain value as pawns disappear.
egthemes.takeaway: Up the exchange: keep pawns on both wings and avoid fortress structures.

egthemes.title: The art of exchanging (Tier 3B checklist) (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Trade the defender's best piece, keep your best attacker, convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage and know what each exchange does.
egthemes.takeaway: Name what the exchange does before you make it.

egthemes.title: Planning, prophylaxis and the king (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Picture the ideal setup first, ask what the opponent wants, improve your worst piece and restrict before you attack.
egthemes.takeaway: Prophylaxis first, then restrict, then attack, and calculate only where the opponent can interfere.

egthemes.title: Transformations and structure-born endgames (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Turn a static advantage into a dynamic one at the right moment, and know which endgames your middlegame structures leave behind.
egthemes.takeaway: Return material or sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition.

egthemes.title: Fortress and anti-fortress (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Test for fortresses before you simplify, know the warning signs and the toolkit for breaking them.
egthemes.takeaway: A large engine evaluation with no visible progress is a fortress alarm.

egthemes.title: Grandmaster technique (level 5)
egthemes.idea: Maximum problems for the opponent, minimum risk for you; repeat once, never three times; know tablebase metrics and build a personal anchor library.
egthemes.takeaway: Calculate backwards from the anchor and choose methods you can execute inside the 50-move horizon.

mgtabs.label: Free / Foundations
mgtabs.tagline: Check every move and make a plan you can trust.

tiers.name: Tier 0 · Foundations
tiers.mission: check every move, find loose pieces and choose a simple plan.
errors: Moving without looking at his last move.
Capturing a pawn and leaving a piece loose.
Attacking with a single piece.
Leaving the king in the centre to grab a pawn.
Seeing a fork square without checking whether the forking piece can be captured.
Trading because it feels simpler, with no reason behind it.

mgtabs.splitRule: Anchor = the Learn puzzle: the easiest puzzle of the chapter. The other puzzles are ordered by rating: the easier half are simple puzzles, the harder half are hard puzzles.

mgtabs.label: Beginner / Speedcourse
mgtabs.tagline: Development, threats, open files and defence.

tiers.name: Tier 1 · Speedcourse
tiers.mission: use a lead in development, make and meet threats, and attack or defend the castled king.
errors: Taking material and handing the tempo back.
Making a threat that he can answer with a move that also threatens you.
Sacrificing without a third attacker.
Placing a rook on an open file where a minor piece can hit it with tempo.
Breaking before your pieces are developed.
Pushing shield pawns in a panic.

mgtabs.splitRule: Anchor = the Learn puzzle: the easiest puzzle of the chapter. The other puzzles are ordered by rating: the easier half are simple puzzles, the harder half are hard puzzles.

mgtabs.label: Intermediate
mgtabs.tagline: Pawn structures, weak squares and the right trades.

tiers.name: Tier 2 · Intermediate
tiers.mission: read the pawn structure and play the plan it asks for.
errors: Preventing everything and building no plan.
White pushes b4–b5 before the rooks and queen are ready.
The owner trades pieces and drifts into a worse endgame.
The owner pushes a pawn with no concrete gain.
Pushing a pawn for no reason and creating a hole.
Trading to relieve tension without a purpose.

mgtabs.splitRule: Anchor = the Learn puzzle: the easiest puzzle of the chapter. The other puzzles are ordered by rating: the easier half are simple puzzles, the harder half are hard puzzles.

mgtabs.label: Advanced
mgtabs.tagline: From imbalances to plans, and the price of every plan.

tiers.name: Tier 3A · Strategic Plans
tiers.mission: turn the imbalances in the position into a plan, and count what each plan costs.
errors: Planning without a tactical scan first.
Mistaking activity for a lasting advantage.
Trading the good bishop and keeping the bad one.
Overextending pawns that then become targets.
Rerouting while he has a strong break available.
Making useful but slow moves in a race.

mgtabs.splitRule: Anchor = the Learn puzzle: the easiest puzzle of the chapter. The other puzzles are ordered by rating: the easier half are simple puzzles, the harder half are hard puzzles.

mgtabs.label: Master / Grandmaster
mgtabs.tagline: Prophylaxis, transformation, initiative and grandmaster decisions.

tiers.name: Tier 3B · Master Technique
tiers.mission: prophylaxis, transformation, initiative and conversion at master level.
errors: Over-prophylaxis, which ends in passivity.
Converting too early or too late.
Sacrificing without permanent compensation.
Sacrificing against a safe, well-developed king.
Simplifying without naming the endgame type.
Playing for mate when a material advantage is enough.

tiers.name: Tier 3C · Grandmaster Synthesis
tiers.mission: run the full MSPC loop on every move, as one system.
errors: Dropping a letter when you are winning.

mgtabs.splitRule: Anchor = the Learn puzzle: the easiest puzzle of the chapter. The other puzzles are ordered by rating: the easier half are simple puzzles, the harder half are hard puzzles.

mgthemes.title: The Blunder Check: Making M Automatic
mgthemes.topic: The Blunder Check: Making M Automatic
mgthemes.idea: Before every move, find out what your opponent's last move did, then check what your own move allows.

mgthemes.title: Loose Pieces and the CCA Scan
mgthemes.topic: Loose Pieces and the CCA Scan
mgthemes.idea: Find every undefended or under-defended piece on the board, then use your Checks, Captures and Attacks to win one before he wins yours.

mgthemes.title: Piece Coordination and Activity
mgthemes.topic: Piece Coordination and Activity
mgthemes.idea: Make every piece work, and bring your least active piece into play before you start an attack.

mgthemes.title: King Safety Basics
mgthemes.topic: King Safety Basics
mgthemes.idea: Castle early, keep the pawns in front of your king where they are, and never open lines toward your own king without a concrete reason.

mgthemes.title: Core Tactical Patterns
mgthemes.topic: Core Tactical Patterns
mgthemes.idea: Learn six geometric patterns until you see them before you calculate: fork, pin, skewer, discovered attack, back-rank mate and removing the defender.

mgthemes.title: Trades, Material and Finding a Simple Plan
mgthemes.topic: Finding and choosing a plan
mgthemes.idea: Trade pieces for a reason, count material honestly, and when nothing is happening improve your worst piece, aim at a weakness or open a line toward his king.

mgthemes.title: Development Lead and the Uncastled King
mgthemes.topic: Development Lead and the Uncastled King
mgthemes.idea: When you lead in development and his king is still in the centre, open the position at once and attack, instead of grabbing material or making slow moves.

mgthemes.title: Direct Threats: Making Them and Meeting Them
mgthemes.topic: Direct Threats: Making Them and Meeting Them
mgthemes.idea: Make threats that improve your position, and meet his threats with the cheapest answer that does not weaken you.

mgthemes.title: Attacking the Castled King: Mating Patterns and the Greek Gift
mgthemes.topic: Attacking the Castled King: Mating Patterns and the Greek Gift
mgthemes.idea: Attack a castled king only when you can bring more attackers than he has defenders, and use the standard mating patterns as your targets.

mgthemes.title: Open Files and the Seventh Rank
mgthemes.topic: Open Files and the Seventh Rank
mgthemes.idea: Put your rooks on open files, double them, and invade the seventh rank, where pawns and the enemy king are weakest.

mgthemes.title: Basic Pawn Breaks: Levers and Opening Lines
mgthemes.topic: Basic Pawn Breaks: Levers and Opening Lines
mgthemes.idea: Use a pawn break to open the lines your pieces need, but only when the break passes a three-part test: purpose, support and safety.

mgthemes.title: Defending Against Attacks
mgthemes.topic: Defending
mgthemes.idea: When he attacks, stay calm: find his real threat, trade his best attackers, and make the fewest weakening moves.

mgthemes.title: Prophylaxis I: What Does My Opponent Want?
mgthemes.topic: Prophylaxis
mgthemes.idea: Before you carry out your plan, ask what your opponent would play if it were his move, and stop it when it is strong.

mgthemes.title: The Carlsbad Structure and the Minority Attack
mgthemes.topic: The Carlsbad Structure and the Minority Attack
mgthemes.idea: In the Carlsbad structure White advances the queenside minority (b4–b5) to create a weakness on c6, while Black counters with a central break or play on the kingside.

mgthemes.title: The Isolated Queen's Pawn (Both Sides)
mgthemes.topic: The Isolated Queen's Pawn (Both Sides)
mgthemes.idea: The owner of the isolated queen's pawn (IQP) attacks while the pieces are still on the board; the opponent blockades the square in front of the pawn and trades pieces toward an endgame.

mgthemes.title: Hanging Pawns
mgthemes.topic: Hanging Pawns
mgthemes.idea: The owner of hanging pawns keeps the pieces active and advances a pawn only when it wins something concrete; the opponent pressures the pawns and tries to force an advance at the wrong moment.

mgthemes.title: Weak Squares, Outposts and Backward Pawns
mgthemes.topic: Weak Squares, Outposts and Backward Pawns
mgthemes.idea: Find the squares and pawns that he can no longer protect with pawns, bring your pieces to them, and guard your own weaknesses the same way.

mgthemes.title: Piece Exchanges: Which Pieces to Trade
mgthemes.topic: Piece Exchanges: Which Pieces to Trade
mgthemes.idea: Trade the pieces that serve your plan, keep the ones that do the work, and before each trade ask what the position looks like after the last recapture.

mgthemes.title: Pawn Chains: The Advance Structure and Attacking the Base
