Pavlovic compares the Meran to the Open Sicilian, and the comparison is exact: sharp, concrete, and unforgiving of general principles. This course gives you the modern main lines and, where a line is genuinely too heavy to learn from a course, says so instead of pretending.

WHAT YOU ADD HERE:
1. The modern Meran with 9.a3 and 11.Qc2 - the current main battleground.
2. The critical Anti-Meran and Catalan set-ups.
3. The Moscow Gambit, which is the upgrade you were promised in the earlier courses.
4. An honest account of which of our positions are equal rather than better.

THE ONE HABIT THAT MATTERS MOST: in every line of this course, ask when to take on c4 and when to break with ...c5. Get those two decisions right and the rest follows.

AN HONEST AUDIT OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

WHERE WE ARE GENUINELY FINE:
- The Meran with 9.a3 and 11...Rc8. Modern, tested, and balanced.
- The Anti-Meran with 6.Qc2. The queen really does end up misplaced on c2.
- The Catalan set-up with 5.g3. Lakdawala is right that White is the one taking a risk.
- The Exchange Slav with 6...Ne4. Not better, but full of play.

WHERE WE ARE EQUAL AND SHOULD BE HAPPY WITH IT:
- The Moscow with 6.Bxf6 Qxf6. We have the bishop pair and no weaknesses. Do not over-press.

WHERE WE MAKE A CONCESSION:
- Against 6.Bh4 we either accept a gambit that demands real study, or we decline and give White a comfortable game. There is no third road. Choose deliberately, and do not pretend the declining line is objectively equal - it is sound, not equalising.

WHERE THE THEORY MOVES FASTEST:
The Meran and the Moscow Gambit. If you take those up, expect to refresh them every year or two. The Exchange Slav, the Catalan set-up and the London lines will still be valid in ten years.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME:
Put your study hours into the lines that do not expire, and use a reliable declining line in the ones that do - unless the sharp line is genuinely your style. A repertoire you maintain badly is worse than a slightly quieter one you know well.

THE THREE THINGS THAT MATTER AT THIS LEVEL:
1. WHEN to play ...dxc4. The same capture is bad on one move and excellent two moves later. Lessons 01 and 03 are entirely about this.
2. WHERE the light-squared bishop belongs. Sometimes f5, sometimes b7, and once neither. Lesson 08 has the exception.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move fourteen. What decides them is whether you recognise the structure in front of you.

1. THE MERAN STRUCTURE (pawns a6-b5-c5 against White's centre).
Plan: ...Bb7, ...a6, then ...c5. After d4-d5 and the exchange on e6, use the f-file and think seriously about castling long.
Do not: hurry ...c5 before ...a6 - the break loses its force.

2. THE MOSCOW STRUCTURE (we own the bishop pair, no weaknesses).
Plan: ...g6 and ...Bg7, then ...e5 or ...c5 at the right moment.
Do not: rush. The bishop pair does not expire; improve a piece and wait.

3. THE DOUBLED g-PAWN STRUCTURE (after Nxg6 hxg6).
Plan: use the open h-file, and remember that f5 and h5 are permanently denied to White.
Do not: think of the doubled pawns as a weakness. You accepted them on purpose.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL EXCHANGE STRUCTURE.
Plan: ...Ne4 and ...f5, or a minority attack with ...b5-b4.
Do not: assume a draw.

THE HABIT TO BUILD: at move fourteen, before calculating anything, name the structure. Then play the plan.

THE BRIDGE TO YOUR WHITE REPERTOIRE: three of these four structures appear in the Colle course from the other side. The e5-outpost you build with White is the outpost you must deny with Black. The Bxh7 sacrifice you look for with White is the one you defuse with ...h6 and ...Nf8. Studying both colours of the same structure is the fastest way to understand it.

The declining line in Lesson 06 and the London treatment in Lesson 09 are practical recommendations for this level rather than book lines.

THE SEMI-SLAV. Look at our pawns: c6, d5 and e6.

WHY THIS FORMATION IS SO GOOD:
1. It is extremely solid. Every pawn is defended by another pawn.
2. It keeps both breaks available: ...c5 hitting the centre, and ...dxc4 followed by ...b5 grabbing queenside space.

The main line. White develops naturally and prepares to castle.

THE MERAN. White refuses to play a waiting move and sends the bishop straight to d3, and that choice has a hidden cost: it hands us a free tempo.
WHY WHITE ACCEPTS THIS: our knight already sits on d7 rather than developing further, and sooner or later we will need the move ...c5 to free our position. In White's mind, the tempo he gives away now with ...dxc4 he gets back later, when we "waste" a move on the c5 break. Keep that trade in mind - it is the logic behind the whole variation.

THE MERAN. Now our plan is fixed and easy to remember:
1. Take on c4 with tempo.
2. Play ...b5 to gain queenside space.
3. Put the bishop on b7, where it finally gets the long diagonal.
4. Break with ...c5 to open the position for our pieces.

That is four moves and one idea. Learn it and you will never be lost in this opening.

WHAT WE HAVE GIVEN UP: our kingside pawn structure and, usually, the right to castle short. Our king often ends up in the centre or on the queenside.
Dreev is explicit in his own preface that the resulting positions are among the most complicated in the entire Semi-Slav complex, and that their final evaluation is still not settled even at grandmaster level - which is precisely why theory here keeps shifting and why memorising a single course line is never going to be enough on its own.
Consolidating the extra pawn. Both of Black's flanks are now weakened - this is a real gambit, not a favour, and Black's compensation has to be earned move by move rather than assumed.

WHY THIS IS WORTH THE RISK: Black is simply a clean pawn ahead, and the practical chances - a future ...b4 hitting c3, ideas of ...Nbd7 challenging the e5-knight, and the latent power of the extra material in any ending - are real enough that top-level Semi-Slav players have staked their reputations on this exact structure for decades.

A NOTE ON DIFFICULTY: this is, by common consent among Semi-Slav specialists, one of the most theoretically demanding positions in the entire repertoire. Treat this course entry as an orientation to the resulting structures and the ideas behind them, not as a substitute for dedicated study of the sharpest lines (10.h4 in particular) before you rely on it in a serious game.

P.Eljanov-A.Dreev, Russian Team Championship 2005.

THE PSYCHOLOGY, and it is worth teaching explicitly: the Exchange Slav player usually wants a short, symmetrical, riskless game. Our whole strategy is to deny him that. Every imbalance we create is worth more than the small objective value it carries.

OUR ANSWER: refuse to co-operate.

This move deliberately unbalances the position. Lakdawala's point is exactly this - against an opponent who wants everything equal and symmetrical, the worst thing we can do is play along.

WHY IT WORKS: the knight on e4 is well placed, it cannot easily be driven away, and it prepares ...e6 with ...Bd6 or ...f5 ideas depending on what White does.

OUR ANSWER: refuse to co-operate.
This move deliberately breaks a well-known opening rule - do not move the same piece twice without a reason - and Lakdawala openly admits it does exactly that. The point is that White cannot easily punish it: he too must spend more time, recapturing on e4 or defending c3, so the "wasted" tempo evens out. What we get instead of a drab, symmetrical Exchange Slav is a livelier, more Grunfeld-like fight, with genuine winning chances for both sides.

WHY THIS MOVE MATTERS: the Exchange Slav has a reputation as a dull, drawish try, and objectively it is - White has committed his structure symmetrically and given up any hope of an opening advantage. The single most important decision Black has in the whole variation is refusing to let the position stay symmetrical and boring. 6...Ne4 does exactly that: it creates immediate imbalance and steers the game toward Grunfeld-like piece activity rather than a lifeless carbon-copy structure.

EDITORIAL NOTE: this particular source game continues with 7...Nxc3, trading down further. Your repertoire instead keeps the knight actively posted on e4 for as long as possible (the line continues 7.e3 e6 8.Bd3 Bd6 9.Bxd6 Qxd6 10.O-O O-O, reaching a position where Black's actively placed pieces and White's slightly compromised structure balance out favourably) - a small, deliberate difference in technique, not a correction of an error. Both approaches are entirely sound; this course teaches the knight-on-e4 version for consistency with the rest of your repertoire's general style of meeting symmetrical structures with maximum piece activity rather than further simplification.

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID.

1. In the Advance, ...e6 before the bishop is out. This is not a small inaccuracy - it is the whole variation thrown away. You reach an Advance French a tempo down, and Lakdawala calls it a clear mistake.

2. In the Advance with 4.dxc5, spending two or three moves recovering the pawn immediately. Develop first. The pawn usually comes back on its own.

3. In the Tartakower, recapturing with the g-pawn. 5...gxf6 is a completely different variation with a different character and much more risk.

4. In the Panov, ...Nc6 instead of ...Nbd7 at the wrong moment, allowing d4-d5 with tempo.

THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:

1. The delayed pin. In the Tartakower, play ...Re8 before ...Bg4 and let White commit to h3. Most opponents play it automatically and hand you a target for the rest of the game.

2. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2 setups and in the Advance with 4.c3, wait until White commits a knight before taking or releasing the tension. The same move is worth much more two moves later.

3. The queen retreat. Against system players, provoking a committal pawn move and then retreating the queen is a real gain, even though it looks like you wasted time. Students hate this - teach it explicitly.

THE HABIT THAT SEPARATES 1600 FROM 2000:
Before every capture and every developing move, ask one question: does this move commit me to something? If yes, can I wait one move and make my opponent commit first?

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR CARO REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move twelve. What decides them is whether you recognise which of these four you are in.

1. THE ADVANCE FRENCH STRUCTURE (pawns e5 vs e6/d5, our bishop OUTSIDE the chain).
Plan: pressure d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6, ...Nf5. Trade the light-squared bishops if you can. Break with ...f6 only when your pieces are ready.
Do not: play ...e6 before the bishop is out. That is the whole variation thrown away.

2. THE TARTAKOWER STRUCTURE (doubled f-pawns, open e-file).
Plan: ...Bd6, ...Re8, ...Nd7-f8, ...Be6, ...Qd7 and play against h3 or with ...f5.
Do not: allow mass exchanges into an endgame. Our structure is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.

3. THE ISOLATED PAWN STRUCTURE (from the Panov).
Plan: survive the middlegame, trade pieces, then attack the pawn. Blockade the square in front of it.
Do not: weaken your king to avoid the initiative. Sit tight - it fades.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL STRUCTURE (from the Exchange).
Plan: create imbalance. ...Ne4, ...b5-b4, or the ...e5 break.
Do not: assume it is a draw. Symmetry is not equality.

THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL HABIT YOU CAN BUILD:
At move twelve, before you calculate anything, ask yourself which of these four structures is on the board. Then play the plan. Most opponents at your level do not do this, and that is where your extra points come from.

THE OTHER ROAD.

Some students never warm to the Tartakower. They dislike the doubled pawns, or they want a structure with no long-term concession at all. This lesson is for them.

WITH 4...Bf5 WE GET: the classical Caro-Kann. Our problem bishop is solved on move four, our structure is completely healthy, and there is nothing to apologise for.

THE CLASSICAL VARIATION - the exact source structure behind your Caro-Kann Classical/Tartakower courses. Black develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before it gets shut in, the single most important structural idea in the whole Caro-Kann.

ESSENTIAL, and automatic. We make h7 available and stop h4-h5-h6.

White trades off Black's most actively placed piece - a real concession of the principle that the side with more space should avoid trades, but justified here since White also gains a tempo toward queenside castling.
Ruling out any future ...Qa5+ tricks, at the cost of blocking the d-file and handing Black's queen a comfortable post on c7.

CASTLING INTO THE STORM, PART TWO. Just as in the Meran (compare Game 01), this looks like it hands White a free attack, but current theory rates Black's chances in the coming opposite-wing race as fully equal. Trust the counterplay: Black's plan is queenside expansion with ...c5, ...Qc7 and ...b5, running exactly as fast as White's kingside pawns.

White commits to the standard plan: f4, g4 and g5, prying open Black's king.

OUR MOVE, AND THE HEART OF THIS COURSE.

WHY WE PLAY IT: we head for a French pawn structure, but WITHOUT the bad bishop. In the French, Black's light-squared bishop gets buried behind pawns on e6 and d5. Here we strike at d4 first, and our bishop still has g4 and f5 available.

Developing actively and preparing quick kingside castling - there is no need for special measures against the King's Indian Attack once Black already controls the centre.
Preparing to meet a future ...dxe4 with tempo, and keeping an eye on the e-file.
White's most testing try, opening the position immediately rather than continuing the slow fianchetto build-up.

EXCERPT NOTE: this reaches a normal isolani middlegame, transposing in spirit to structures you already know well from the Panov and Semi-Slav branches of your repertoire - the same plans (pressure down the c- and e-files, trading down toward a favourable minor-piece ending) apply directly.

TAKEAWAY: the King's Indian Attack is not a system to fear. Meeting it with an early, well-timed ...e5 turns White's quiet set-up into an open isolani position where Black's activity and structural soundness generally outweigh White's slightly easier development.

I.Glek-A.Dreev, European Club Cup, Saint Vincent 2005.

S.name: Specifics
S.text: What makes this position unique: the game phase, the pawn structure, weaknesses, targets and what your repertoire’s structure asks for.

C.name: Calculation
C.text: Calculate your candidates to the end, including every reply your opponent has. No stopping halfway out of fear. Also include what you miscalculated or missed.

middlegameMasterclass.courseTitle: The Middlegame Masterclass: From Zero to Grandmaster

chapters.chapterName: The Blunder Check: Making M Automatic
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Before every move, find out what your opponent's last move did, then check what your own move allows.

Most games at this level end with one unforced error: a piece left where it could be taken, or a threat nobody noticed. This chapter makes the check automatic, so the rest of the course has a safe floor to stand on.

M — Move
- Direct threat: look at the square his piece landed on and trace every line from it: rank, file, diagonal and knight jumps. Does it attack anything of yours, or give check?
- Immediate plan: ask what the move prepares. A bishop aimed at your king's diagonal or a rook on an open file is usually step one of something larger.
- New weaknesses: look at the square he left and at the pieces he stopped defending. A move can open a line for a piece standing behind it, and it can leave a neighbour unprotected.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. At this level, count for both sides which pieces are attacked, which are defended and which are neither.

Alarm Triggers — run the full check when:
- his last move put a piece on a square that attacks yours or gives check,
- his last move opened a line, because a piece left a rank, file or diagonal,
- his pieces stand near your king or aim at the squares around it,
- one of your pieces is attacked by something worth less, or is attacked more times than it is defended.

Counter-Alarms — your own move is about to blunder when:
- the piece you want to move is currently defending something,
- your move leaves any piece with no defender,
- you think 'he probably won't see it',
- the position looks calm and you are moving fast.

Pattern in practice. He moves a bishop onto a diagonal that points at your queen, with your knight as the only piece in between. M tells you the knight is pinned. Any plan that needs that knight to move, or leaves the queen undefended, now fails.

P — Priorities
When his move creates a threat, answer in this order:
1. If he threatens checkmate, deal with that first.
2. Capture the attacker, if it is safe.
3. Move the attacked piece to a useful square.
4. Defend the piece or block the line.
5. Counter-attack with a bigger threat, only after you have calculated it.
If there is no threat, go to your own CCA scan (chapter 0.2).

C — Calculation
The Two-Question Blunder Check, run on your intended move before you let go of the piece:
1. After my move, what can he capture? Count attackers and defenders on every piece of mine that is attacked.
2. After my move, what checks and attacks does he have? Look for forks and discovered attacks, not only captures.
Depth is one move for him and your reply. If the move survives both questions, play it.

Common mistakes
- Moving without looking at his last move.
- Hope chess: playing a move that only works if he misses something.
- Forgetting that the piece you moved was a defender.
- Checking only your own plan and never his answers.

chapters.chapterName: Loose Pieces and the CCA Scan
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Find every undefended or under-defended piece on the board, then use your Checks, Captures and Attacks to win one before he wins yours.

The old saying 'loose pieces drop off' is true at every level, and below 800 it decides most games. The scan that wins his piece is the same scan that protects yours.

M — Move
- Direct threat: which of my pieces does his move attack, and is each one defended enough?
- Immediate plan: is he adding a second attacker to a piece he already attacks once?
- New weaknesses: which of his pieces lost its defender when he moved? Developing a piece or pushing a pawn often leaves something loose behind.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. A piece is loose if nothing defends it. It is under-defended if it is attacked more times than it is defended, or attacked by a cheaper piece. Values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9.

Alarm Triggers — start the CCA scan when:
- a piece of his has no defender and one of your pieces can attack it with tempo,
- two of his pieces stand on one rank, file or diagonal, or a knight-jump apart, so one move may attack both,
- his defender is pinned, overloaded (guarding two things) or has just moved away,
- his queen stands on a square that one of your cheaper pieces can attack.

Counter-Alarms — he is doing it to you when:
- one of your pieces has no defender, especially on the rim or deep in his territory,
- two of your pieces stand in a line, which is fork or skewer geometry,
- the only defender of one piece is also needed somewhere else.

P — Priorities
The CCA scan, in this order:
1. Checks: list every one. Even an odd-looking check can win a loose piece or drive the king.
2. Captures: list every capture, including captures of defended pieces, then count the exchange.
3. Attacks: list every move that attacks a loose piece or two things at once.
Then run the same scan for him on the position after your candidate move: his checks, his captures, his attacks.

C — Calculation
- Count attackers and defenders on the target square. Capture with the cheapest piece first.
- Play the exchange to the end. After the last recapture, are you ahead? If the next capture loses material, stop before it.
- Before taking a free piece, ask whether it is bait: after the capture, which checks and captures does he have?
- After your move, run the Two-Question Blunder Check from chapter 0.1.

Common mistakes
- Capturing a pawn and leaving a piece loose.
- Attacking a piece without noticing that the attacker itself is loose.
- Counting the first capture but not the recapture.
- Forgetting the in-between move: a check or capture he can insert before he recaptures.

chapters.chapterName: Piece Coordination and Activity
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Make every piece work, and bring your least active piece into play before you start an attack.

A piece is worth more on a good square than on a bad one. Pieces coordinate when they protect each other and attack the same target, and a lone attacker is usually driven away.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move attack anything, or take a square away from one of my pieces?
- Immediate plan: is he bringing another piece toward my king or toward a target? Count how many of his pieces point at one area.
- New weaknesses: has he left a piece out of play or a rook disconnected? That is where his position is soft.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Development (all minor pieces off the back rank), connected rooks (nothing between them), a castled king, knights on central squares, bishops on open diagonals, and a queen that cannot be harassed. Your worst piece is the one with the fewest useful squares.

Alarm Triggers — improve coordination when:
- a piece has not moved for several turns: it is your worst piece, so bring it in,
- your rooks are not connected and the king is still in the centre: finish development first,
- a knight stands on the rim (a- or h-file) with no target,
- a bishop is blocked by its own pawns,
- your pieces stand on one side of the board and the action is on the other.

Counter-Alarms — he is out-coordinating you when:
- all his pieces aim at one area (your king or a weak pawn) while yours stand elsewhere,
- he has castled and connected his rooks while you have not,
- he can attack a target with three pieces and you can defend it with one.

P — Priorities
Checks, captures and attacks only work when the pieces are coordinated, so rank your quiet moves:
1. Finish development: minor pieces out, then castle.
2. Connect the rooks.
3. Put rooks on open or half-open files.
4. Improve the worst piece.
Do not move the same piece twice in the opening unless it wins something or meets a threat.

C — Calculation
- Safety: after the move, is the piece defended, and can a cheaper piece attack it?
- Value: does the piece control more useful squares after the move than before?
- Cooperation: does it defend or support another piece?
- Then run the Two-Question Blunder Check from chapter 0.1.

Common mistakes
- Attacking with a single piece.
- Moving one piece again and again while the others sleep.
- Bringing the queen out early and losing time when it is harassed.
- Leaving rooks on closed files for the whole game.

Opening Bridge
Each repertoire in the library is a coordination blueprint. [W-Colle] White builds pawns on d4, c3 and e3 and puts the pieces behind them: Bd3 and Nbd2 support the later e3–e4 break, Nf3 guards the centre, and the king castles. [B-CK and B-Slav] In the Classical Caro-Kann and the Slav, Black develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before playing ...e6. In Meran-type Semi-Slav lines the same bishop is freed by ...dxc4, ...b5 and ...Bb7. When your pieces reach those squares, development is done and the middlegame plan can start.

chapters.chapterName: King Safety Basics
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Castle early, keep the pawns in front of your king where they are, and never open lines toward your own king without a concrete reason.

The king decides the game. Most checkmates at this level happen because the king stayed in the centre or because the pawn shield was weakened for no reason.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move give check, or threaten a check that wins something?
- Immediate plan: are his queen, bishops or rooks lining up on the squares around my king, especially h7 or h2, g7 or g2, f7 or f2?
- New weaknesses: has he pushed the pawns in front of his own king, or left the king in the centre? That is where he is soft.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Castled or not. The f, g and h pawns unmoved. A luft square, which is a flight square made by moving one of those pawns one step. Open and half-open files facing the king. His attackers near the king against your defenders.

Back-rank pattern. The king stands on g1 behind unmoved f2, g2 and h2 pawns with no luft. An enemy rook or queen reaches the first rank on an open file, and the king is mated.

Alarm Triggers — act on your king when:
- your king is still on e1 or e8 and a central file is opening: castle now,
- his queen and a bishop aim at the same square next to your king (a battery),
- an open file points at your king and he has a rook to put on it,
- your back rank has no luft and one of his rooks controls an open file,
- you are about to push a pawn in front of your castled king 'to attack something'.

Counter-Alarms — his king is the target when:
- his king is uncastled and files are opening (see chapter 1.1),
- his shield pawns have moved,
- his back rank has no luft and one of your rooks can reach it.

P — Priorities
1. Castle before you attack, unless a forcing line wins at once.
2. When he threatens your king, remove or block the attacker before you pursue your own plan.
3. Make luft (h3 or h6, or g3 or g6) when an enemy rook can reach your back rank.
4. Keep the f, g and h pawns at home unless a concrete reason, such as a break or a defensive need, says otherwise.

C — Calculation
The king-safety scan, before each move:
- Which squares next to my king does he attack, and with what?
- Can he give check next move? Where would my king go?
- If I move the pawn or piece in front of my king, which line opens?
- Count his attackers against my defenders near the king. If he has more, defend or trade before you attack.

Common mistakes
- Leaving the king in the centre to grab a pawn.
- Pushing the g- and h-pawns for a pawn storm while his pieces are ready to punish it.
- Forgetting the back rank.
- Castling into a position where his pieces already aim at the king.

Opening Bridge
[W-Colle] White castles kingside early, and Bd3 and Nf3 sit on the attacking squares. Black's bishop on d6 aims at h2 along the b8–h2 diagonal, and the knight on f3 guards h2, so check h2 before that knight leaves f3. [B-CK and B-Slav] Black castles kingside after ...e6 and ...Be7 or ...Bd6. Some Semi-Slav lines in the Black repertoire push the g- and h-pawns on purpose. Those pushes are justified by concrete calculation, which is exactly the kind of exception Tier 3B teaches.

chapters.chapterName: Core Tactical Patterns
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Learn six geometric patterns until you see them before you calculate: fork, pin, skewer, discovered attack, back-rank mate and removing the defender.

Tactics are not luck. Each pattern needs the same few ingredients on the board, and once you know them you can see the pattern coming from the position.

The six patterns. For each: what happens, the Alarm Trigger to look for, and a quick test.
- Fork. One piece attacks two targets at once. Look for two enemy pieces, or a king and a piece, a knight-jump apart or on one line from a square you can reach. Quick test: is the forking piece safe on that square?
- Pin. A piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it; an absolute pin is against the king. Look for an enemy piece on one line with its king or queen, and your bishop, rook or queen able to reach that line. Quick test: can you attack the pinned piece again?
- Skewer. A valuable piece must move and exposes a lesser piece behind it. Look for an enemy king or queen on a line with another piece behind it. Quick test: must the front piece really move?
- Discovered attack. Moving one piece opens a line for another. Look for your rook, bishop or queen standing behind your own piece on a line aimed at a target. Quick test: does the moving piece make a threat of its own? A discovered check is the strongest version.
- Back-rank mate. A rook or queen mates a king trapped by its own pawns. Look for a king with no luft, an open file to the back rank and no defenders. Quick test: are all the king's squares covered or blocked?
- Removing the defender. Capture or chase away the piece that guards a target. Look for a defender that is loose, pinned or guarding two things. Quick test: after the defender goes, does the target fall?

M — Move
- Direct threat: did his move set up one of the six patterns against me, such as a knight a jump from a fork square or a pin on my queen?
- Immediate plan: is he lining up pieces on one line?
- New weaknesses: which of his pieces now stand on a line or a fork square? His last move may have handed you a pattern.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Pieces on a common line, undefended pieces, pieces that defend two things, kings without luft.

Alarm Triggers. The pattern list above is your trigger list. Add one general rule: whenever two enemy pieces share a line, or one enemy piece guards two things, a pattern is probably near.

Counter-Alarms — a pattern is aimed at you when:
- your king and queen, or your king and a rook, stand on one line,
- a knight can land on a square that attacks two of your pieces,
- one of your pieces guards two things at once,
- your king has no luft and a file is open.

P — Priorities
Search in this order: patterns that begin with check, then patterns that win material by capture, and quiet double attacks last. A forcing pattern leaves him fewer replies.

C — Calculation
1. Name the pattern.
2. Confirm the geometry: are all the lines clear?
3. Check that the key piece is safe on its new square.
4. Count the material after the pattern runs its course.
5. Look for his in-between move, which is usually a check or a capture.

Common mistakes
- Seeing a fork square without checking whether the forking piece can be captured.
- Treating a relative pin as absolute: the pinned piece may still move if the exchange favours him.
- Forgetting that a discovered attack also frees the moving piece to make its own threat.
- Trying a back-rank mate without checking for a defender.

chapters.chapterName: Trades, Material and Finding a Simple Plan
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Trade pieces for a reason, count material honestly, and when nothing is happening improve your worst piece, aim at a weakness or open a line toward his king.

M — Move
- Direct threat: is his trade offer a real threat, or just an exchange I can accept or decline?
- Immediate plan: what does he gain after the trade, such as a better structure, an open file or a safer king?
- New weaknesses: which squares or pawns become weak after the trade, mine or his?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Material count (1, 3, 3, 5, 9), king safety for both sides, which pieces are active, and any damage to the pawn structure.

Trading rules for this tier.
- Ahead in material: trade pieces, not pawns.
- Behind in material: avoid trades and keep pieces on for tricks.
- Cramped: trade to get room.
- Attacked: trade the most dangerous attacker.
- Trade your passive piece for his active one, not the other way round.

Alarm Triggers — trade when:
- you are ahead and your king is safe,
- you are cramped and a trade frees one of your pieces,
- his most dangerous attacker can be exchanged,
- the trade would double or isolate his pawns.

Counter-Alarms — decline or re-check when:
- his king is exposed and you have attackers: keep the pieces on,
- a trade offer opens a file toward your king or wrecks your pawn structure,
- you are behind and he offers trade after trade.

P — Priorities
When nothing is forcing, choose a plan from the Three Sources, after king safety and development are done:
1. Worst piece: find your least active piece and bring it to a better square.
2. Weak target: find a pawn or piece that several of your pieces can attack.
3. Line to the king: open a file or diagonal toward his king with a pawn break, but only if your own king is safe.

C — Calculation
- Before a trade: after the last recapture, what is the material? Whose king is safer? Whose pawn structure is better? Which pieces remain?
- Before a quiet move: run the Two-Question Blunder Check from chapter 0.1.

Common mistakes
- Trading because it feels simpler, with no reason behind it.
- Trading your best piece for his worst.
- Counting the pieces and forgetting the pawn structure.
- Making random moves when nothing is forced, instead of using the Three Sources.

Opening Bridge
All three repertoires reach positions where nothing is forced once development is done. Use the Three Sources there. The worst piece is usually the one that has not yet reached its repertoire square, the weak target is often a pawn on a half-open file, and the pawn break (e3–e4 in the Colle, ...c5 in the Caro-Kann and Slav) is the lever each repertoire is built around. Chapter 1.5 covers those breaks.

chapters.chapterName: Development Lead and the Uncastled King
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. When you lead in development and his king is still in the centre, open the position at once and attack, instead of grabbing material or making slow moves.

Development is a form of time. Each piece you bring into play without him matching it is a tempo in hand, and tempi cash in fastest when lines are open and the king has not castled.

M — Move
- Direct threat: what does his move attack? A king in the centre rarely has time to make threats of its own.
- Immediate plan: is he trying to castle, to trade queens or to close the centre to buy time?
- New weaknesses: look for pawn grabs, queen moves and repeated moves with the same piece. Each one costs a tempo and often leaves f7 or f2, or the e-file, loose.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Pieces developed on each side, castling rights, open and half-open central files, the squares f7 and f2 (the weakest points before castling), and whether his queen is out of play.

Alarm Triggers — attack when:
- his king is still in the centre (e8 or e1) and he has not castled,
- you have at least two more developed pieces than he does,
- a central file (d or e) is open, half-open or can be opened with a pawn lever,
- your pieces aim at f7 or f2, or at the squares next to his king,
- he has spent tempi on pawn grabs, queen moves or repeated piece moves.

Counter-Alarms — you are the one in danger when:
- your own king is uncastled and he is better developed: castle first and do not open the centre,
- he offers a pawn that would drag your queen or a minor piece away from the fight,
- he can open a file toward your king with a lever and you are behind in development.

Reference game. Morphy's Opera Game (Paris, 1858) is the classic model of a development lead turned into an attack on an uncastled king, finished by a queen sacrifice and a rook mate on d8. Pull the PGN from your database before using it.

P — Priorities
1. Checks that drive the king or gain a tempo.
2. Captures that open lines or remove the defender of a key square, including a pawn or piece sacrifice when it opens the centre toward the king.
3. Attacks that add a piece to the attack with tempo, aimed at f7 or f2 or at the open file.
4. If nothing is forcing: castle, connect the rooks and put a rook on the open file before you create new targets.
Do not trade queens while his king is exposed. Trade his defenders instead.

C — Calculation
- Count attackers: how many of your pieces can reach the king zone, against how many defenders he has?
- List his escape squares: can the king run, castle or hide behind a blocker?
- Calculate every check first, then every capture that opens lines. Stop when the position is quiet or he is mated.
- Compare what you give with the damage you do. A sacrifice is justified only if the line ends in mate, a winning material count or an attack he cannot meet.
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check on the last move of the line.

Common mistakes
- Taking material and handing the tempo back.
- Delaying castling because the attack looks good.
- Attacking with two pieces while the rest are undeveloped.
- Trading queens, which ends the attack.
- Opening the centre while your own king is uncastled.

Opening Bridge
[W-Colle] The Colle develops fast and castles early, so you seldom face this plan. Your chance comes when Black delays castling to chase pawns: then e3–e4 opens the centre while the king is still there. [B-CK and B-Slav] Black's structure (c6, d5, e6) and early castling are designed to deny White this plan. If White grabs a pawn or sorties with the queen, answer with development and a central break.

chapters.chapterName: Direct Threats: Making Them and Meeting Them
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Make threats that improve your position, and meet his threats with the cheapest answer that does not weaken you.

A threat is a move that wins something if the opponent ignores it. The side that makes threats chooses where the game is played; the side that only answers them is always one move behind.

M — Move
- Direct threat: name his threat precisely. What exactly does he win if you pass? A capture, a check, a mate, a fork?
- Immediate plan: is this threat a one-off, or the first of a series?
- New weaknesses: what did he leave undefended to make the threat? Every threat has a price, and the price is a weakness.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Loose pieces, kings with few flight squares, pieces that can move with tempo (with check or with an attack), pins and overloaded defenders.

Alarm Triggers — make a threat when:
- one of his pieces is loose, or defended only by a piece you can attack,
- his king has few flight squares and one of your pieces can attack it,
- a developing move can also attack something, so you gain a tempo,
- one move can create two threats at once, which is a double threat.

Counter-Alarms — your answer needs extra care when:
- he makes a threat with a move that also develops or improves his position,
- he threatens two things at once,
- your natural answer would block your own piece, weaken your king or leave another piece loose.

The five answers to a threat. Capture the attacker, move the attacked piece, defend it, block the line, or counter-attack with a bigger threat. Use the cheapest one that works.

P — Priorities
1. Checks that win material or a tempo.
2. Captures that remove a defender, or the attacker of your piece.
3. Attacks that create a double threat, or that gain a tempo on a developing move.
When you are the one under threat, first look for a safe counter that makes a bigger threat. If there is none, use the five answers in order of cost, and prefer the answer that also improves your position.

C — Calculation
- Forcing lines first: for each check, capture or threat, list his legal answers and calculate the best one, not the one you hope for.
- Double-threat test: after your move, can he parry both threats with one move? If so, you have only a single threat.
- Safety of the threatening piece: can he chase it away and gain a tempo?
- Calculate two or three moves deep to a quiet position, then run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- Making a threat that he can answer with a move that also threatens you.
- Moving a piece to a square where it can be hit with tempo.
- Answering every threat with a retreat and losing the initiative for good.
- Counter-attacking without counting: a counter-threat smaller than his loses.

Opening Bridge
The opening lines in all three repertoires already contain threats in miniature: a developing bishop that attacks a pawn, a pawn move that attacks a piece. The habit this chapter builds is to ask on every move which of those threats is real, and which answer costs the least.

chapters.chapterName: Attacking the Castled King: Mating Patterns and the Greek Gift
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Attack a castled king only when you can bring more attackers than he has defenders, and use the standard mating patterns as your targets.

One piece rarely breaks a castled king, and three pieces often do. The patterns below tell you which squares to aim at and which defenders to remove first.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move threaten my king, or does it ignore the danger?
- Immediate plan: is he trying to trade off my attackers, above all the queen?
- New weaknesses: has he moved a defender away from the king (the knight from f6, the bishop from e7 or d6), pushed a pawn in front of the king, or let the shield thin out? That is your trigger.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. The pawn shield (f, g, h), the defenders near the king (a knight on f6, a bishop on e7, the queen), open and half-open files toward the king, the b1–h7 diagonal for White and its mirror for Black, and which of your pieces can reach the king zone.

The mating patterns. For each: the idea and the Alarm Trigger to look for.
- Greek Gift (Bxh7+). Sacrifice the bishop on h7, then Ng5+ and Qh5. Look for the five conditions in the checklist below.
- Queen and knight on h7. The queen mates on h7 with a knight on g5 supporting her. Look for an open diagonal to h7, a knight that can reach g5, and the king's own rook on f8 blocking the escape square.
- Back-rank mate. A rook or queen mates on the first or eighth rank. Look for no luft, an open file to the back rank and defenders missing.
- Smothered mate. A knight mates a king hemmed in by its own pieces. Look for a king on h8 or h1 with pawns beside it, a knight that can reach f7 or f2, and a queen check that forces the rook to capture (Qg8+ Rxg8 Nf7#).
- Rook lift and h-file attack. A rook swings up to the third rank, then to the h-file. Look for an open or half-open h-file and a rook that can reach the third rank safely.

The Greek Gift checklist. Check all five before you play Bxh7+.
1. The bishop attacks h7 along the b1–h7 diagonal (normally from d3), and nothing blocks it: no pawn on e4, f5 or g6.
2. A knight can jump to g5 with check (normally from f3), and nothing can capture it there: no bishop on e7, no queen on d8 with an open diagonal, no knight on e6, no pawn on f6 or h6.
3. Your queen can reach h5 in one move after Ng5+. From d1 she needs e2 and f3 empty, and f3 empties when the knight jumps.
4. Black's knight on f6 is absent, pinned or driven away. A knight on f6 captures on h7 or h5 and ends the attack. A pawn push such as e4–e5 is the usual way to drive it away.
5. A third attacker or a forced finish exists, such as a rook that can lift to the third rank or a pawn on e5 that takes squares away from his defenders, so that the threat of Qh7# cannot be met without losing material.

Typical flow. 1.Bxh7+ Kxh7 2.Ng5+ followed by Qh5, threatening Qh7#. Calculate every king move (Kg8, Kg6, Kh6, Kh8) and every defensive resource, such as ...Re8 giving the king the f8 square, ...f5, or ...Qxg5 when the queen can reach g5.

Counter-Alarms — the Greek Gift is off, or you are the target, when:
- a condition on the checklist fails, such as a knight on f6, a bishop on e7 or a pawn on h6,
- he has more pieces near your king than you have defenders,
- your own knight leaves f3, so h2 loses its defender while his bishop on d6 or his queen points at h2.

Reference game. Lasker–Bauer (Amsterdam, 1889) is the classic double bishop sacrifice on h7 and g7. Pull the PGN from your database before using it.

P — Priorities
1. Checks: the sacrifice itself is a check, and the follow-up checks must keep the initiative.
2. Captures: remove the defender of the key square first (for example the knight on f6), and sacrifice only when the remaining defenders cannot cope.
3. Attacks: add reserves before the sacrifice, such as a queen on the diagonal, a rook on the e-file or a rook lift, as long as he has no time to defend.

C — Calculation
- Count his defenders and your attackers in the king zone, move by move.
- Calculate the sacrifice to the end: all his king moves and his best defensive try.
- Check the in-between moves, especially a check that wins a tempo.
- Check your own king. When the knight leaves f3, h2 loses a defender, and a black bishop on d6 or a queen may capture there with check.
- Compare the end of the line with what you gave: mate, or a clearly winning material count. If you cannot see one, do not sacrifice.

Common mistakes
- Sacrificing without a third attacker.
- Ignoring ...Bxh2+ or ...Qxg5 after the knight jumps.
- Missing that a pawn on h6 or a bishop on e7 shuts the Greek Gift down.
- Playing the sacrifice before the knight on f6 is gone.

Opening Bridge
[W-Colle] The Colle is built for this plan. Bd3 aims at h7, Nf3 is ready to jump to g5, and with the pawn on e3 the queen reaches h5 along the d1–h5 diagonal once the knight leaves f3. The push e3–e4–e5 is the usual way to drive a knight away from f6, which is condition four. Check the exact move orders in the Colle-Koltanowski PGN and the Model Games Encyclopedia, because the final positions decide which conditions hold. [B-CK and B-Slav] Black defends the same geometry. A knight on f6 together with ...h6 or a bishop on e7 shuts the Greek Gift down, so learn to recognise when your opponent's structure allows it.

chapters.chapterName: Open Files and the Seventh Rank
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Put your rooks on open files, double them, and invade the seventh rank, where pawns and the enemy king are weakest.

An open file is a highway for rooks. The side that controls it decides where the rooks can enter the enemy position.

M — Move
- Direct threat: can his rook use that file, or the seventh rank, against me?
- Immediate plan: is he doubling rooks, contesting my file or preparing to trade rooks?
- New weaknesses: did he leave a file, a seventh-rank pawn or his back rank unguarded?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. An open file has no pawns. A half-open file has only an enemy pawn on it. Entry squares are the squares where a rook can land on the file or on the seventh rank, such as c7, d7, c2 and d2, and the minor pieces and pawns that guard them. The seventh rank is rank 7 for White and rank 2 for Black.

Alarm Triggers — take the file when:
- a file is open and you can occupy it first,
- a half-open file points at a weak or backward pawn,
- your rooks are connected and can double,
- the entry square is not covered by an enemy pawn or minor piece,
- his king sits on the back rank, or his seventh-rank pawns are loose.

Counter-Alarms — he is taking the file when:
- he has a rook on an open file and the entry squares on your side are uncovered,
- your rooks stand passive on closed files,
- one of his rooks can reach your second rank.

P — Priorities
1. Checks along the file or along the seventh rank.
2. Captures: win the seventh-rank pawns from behind, or capture a defender of the entry square.
3. Attacks: double the rooks, or threaten mate on the back rank.
Contest a file only when you can support your rook there. Trade a pair of rooks when that leaves you with the only rook on the file.

C — Calculation
- Entry-square safety: is the square attacked by a minor piece or a pawn?
- Trap check: a rook on the seventh can be trapped by a king and a minor piece, so check the retreat squares before you go in.
- Back-rank check for your own king whenever your rooks leave the first rank.
- Doubling check: is the second rook defended, and can he trade into an endgame that favours him?

Common mistakes
- Placing a rook on an open file where a minor piece can hit it with tempo.
- Trading the only rook that controlled the file.
- Invading the seventh rank with one rook that can be trapped.
- Leaving your own back rank weak when your rooks go forward.

Opening Bridge
[B-Slav] The Exchange Slav (cxd5 cxd5) leaves the c-file completely open, so the fight for the file starts early. Apply the triggers above to see who controls it and who gets the entry square first. [B-CK] In the Panov-Botvinnik with 5...e6, once the c-pawns are exchanged and Black recaptures on d5 with the knight, the c-file is open and White's d4 pawn is isolated. The rook fight for the c-file is part of the plan, and chapter 2.3 builds on it.

chapters.chapterName: Basic Pawn Breaks: Levers and Opening Lines
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Use a pawn break to open the lines your pieces need, but only when the break passes a three-part test: purpose, support and safety.

A pawn break is a pawn move that challenges an enemy pawn so that lines open or the structure changes. Pieces want open lines, and breaks are how you create them.

Common breaks.
- e3–e4 for White: opens the centre and frees the pieces; the central lever of the Colle.
- ...c5 for Black: challenges d4; the lever of the Caro-Kann Advance and of Slav and Semi-Slav structures.
- ...e5 for Black: challenges d4 and wins central space.
- f2–f4 or ...f7–f5: opens the f-file toward the king, at the price of weakening your own king.
- b2–b4 or ...b7–b5 with a-pawn support: opens the queenside; see chapter 2.2.

The three-part break test.
1. Purpose: which line, square or target does the break open?
2. Support: after the exchanges on the break square, do you have at least as many pieces and pawns supporting it as he has attacking it?
3. Safety: what does it loosen: the squares behind the pawn, your king's cover, a piece that the pawn was defending?

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move threaten a break, or take support away from mine?
- Immediate plan: which break is he preparing? Look at where his pieces and pawns are massing.
- New weaknesses: which squares behind his pawns become weak if he breaks?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. The break squares for both sides, the attackers and defenders of the pawn you will challenge, the files and diagonals the break would open, and the position of both kings.

Alarm Triggers — break when:
- your pieces are developed and your king is safe,
- the break square is supported by at least as many pieces as attack it,
- the break opens a file or diagonal toward his king or a weakness,
- you are cramped and the break frees your pieces,
- he is less developed, because open lines favour the better-developed side.

Counter-Alarms — he is about to break when:
- his pieces stand behind the break pawn and support it,
- you cannot contest the break square with enough pieces,
- the break would open a file toward your king while your pieces are not ready.

P — Priorities
1. If the break attacks a piece, so that it comes with tempo, play it at once.
2. Otherwise prepare it with a developing move that adds support.
3. If his break hurts you, prevent it. If it does not, ignore it and continue your plan.

C — Calculation
- Count the exchanges on the break square step by step: pawn takes, who recaptures, who ends up with the pawn or the open file?
- After the break, check the new lines for both kings and for loose pieces.
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check on the position after the exchanges.

Common mistakes
- Breaking before your pieces are developed.
- Breaking when he is better developed, which hands him the open lines.
- Creating an isolated pawn with no compensation.
- Ignoring his break until it is too late.

Opening Bridge
[W-Colle] The e3–e4 break is the central lever. Bd3 and Nbd2 support it, and it usually comes after castling. If Black captures on e4, White recaptures and the pieces point at the kingside. If Black does not capture, e4–e5 gains space and drives a knight from f6. Check the exact order in the Colle-Koltanowski PGN. [B-CK] In the Advance structure the lever is ...c5, which attacks the base of White's chain at d4 (chapter 2.7). [B-Slav] The levers are ...c5 and ...e5, and in Meran-type lines ...b5 and ...c5.

chapters.chapterName: Defending Against Attacks
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. When he attacks, stay calm: find his real threat, trade his best attackers, and make the fewest weakening moves.

Panic is the real enemy in defence. A calm count of attackers and defenders usually shows that the position holds, or shows exactly which piece must be traded.

M — Move
- Direct threat: what is the concrete threat right now? A mate threat, a capture, a pin?
- Immediate plan: which pieces is he adding to the attack? Count them.
- New weaknesses: what did he leave behind? An attack usually leaves his own king or pieces loose, and that is your counterplay.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Attackers against defenders around the king, open lines, the pawn shield, escape squares, and your counter-chances.

Alarm Triggers — switch to defence when:
- he has more pieces near your king than you have defenders,
- an open file or diagonal points at your king,
- his queen and another piece aim at the same square next to your king,
- he can sacrifice on h7, h2, g7 or g2 and you cannot refute it.

Counter-Alarms — his attack is running out of steam when:
- his queen is his only attacker,
- you can trade his most dangerous piece,
- his own king is exposed or his pieces are loose.

The four defensive tools.
- Trade the attackers, above all the queen.
- Control the key squares: add a defender or block the line.
- Make luft or move the king when that is safer.
- Counter-attack, but only when your threat is bigger and faster than his.

P — Priorities
1. Checks: your own checks, when they win a tempo or a piece. A counter-check can break an attack.
2. Captures: capture the attacking piece or a key supporting piece.
3. Attacks: a counter-threat if you have one. If not, add a defender.
Beginner rule: do not push the pawns in front of your king in a panic. Each push weakens a square that his pieces can use.

C — Calculation
- For each defensive move, list his best attacking reply: his checks, captures and attacks.
- Check for overloaded defenders, meaning one piece guarding two things.
- Test the sacrifice on the key square (h7, h2, g7 or g2) by counting attackers and defenders before you rely on the defence.
- Finish with the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- Pushing shield pawns in a panic.
- Defending with a piece that is needed elsewhere.
- Missing a counter-attack that is available.
- Refusing to trade queens when his attack is strong.

Opening Bridge
The repertoire structures are solid shells: pawns on c3 and e3 for White, pawns on c6 and e6 for Black. Those shells let you defend by trading attackers instead of pushing pawns. Practise the habit against the typical attackers in each line, which are the opposing bishop aimed at your king and the queen coming to the kingside.

chapters.chapterName: Prophylaxis I: What Does My Opponent Want?
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Before you carry out your plan, ask what your opponent would play if it were his move, and stop it when it is strong.

Prophylaxis means preventing the opponent's ideas. At this tier it is a question, not yet a style: you ask it on quiet moves, and you act on the answer only when his idea is dangerous. There are three possible answers: prevent his idea directly, allow it because you have a prepared reply, or make a bigger threat of your own.

M — Move
- Direct threat: what does his last move threaten right now?
- Immediate plan: what does it prepare over the next two or three moves? A pawn move often prepares a piece route or a break.
- New weaknesses: what does the move give up? The same move can prepare his plan and weaken him at the same time.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. His pawn breaks, his outpost squares, the squares his best piece wants, his tactical ideas (forks, pins), and the number of moves your own plan needs.

Alarm Triggers — stop and ask 'what does he want?' when:
- the position is quiet and he has an obvious improving move, such as a piece to an outpost or a pawn break,
- his last move was preparatory, for example a bishop placed to aim at h2 or a pawn move that prepares ...c5,
- your plan needs three or more moves and his idea needs fewer,
- a square on your side of the board has become available to his knight,
- one of his pawn breaks is a single move from being playable.

Counter-Alarms — you are overdoing it when:
- you prevent an idea that does not hurt you,
- you have a forcing win and choose a quiet move instead,
- every move you make is a reaction.

P — Priorities
1. Forcing moves come first: if you have a CCA that wins, play it. Prophylaxis never replaces a winning tactic.
2. Next, a move that prevents his idea and improves your position at the same time.
3. Last, a plain plan move, when his idea is harmless.

C — Calculation
- Replacement test: sit in his seat and ask which move you would play. That move is his main idea.
- For each candidate, find his best reply and compare: does your move leave him a good one?
- Calculate his idea before you prevent it. Not every idea is a threat.
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- Preventing everything and building no plan.
- Preventing an imaginary threat while a real one stands on the board.
- Ignoring his idea because your own plan is exciting.
- Using prophylaxis as an excuse to play passively when a forcing line exists.

Opening Bridge
[B-CK] In the Classical lines, ...h6 after White's h4 is prophylaxis in action: it gives the bishop on g6 the h7 square when White plays h4–h5. Name the idea behind every small pawn move in your repertoire. [W-Colle] Typical Black ideas against the Colle are ...e5, ...c4 hitting the bishop on d3, and a bishop on d6 pressing on h2. Ask which of them is actually strong in the position before you continue with your own plan.

chapters.chapterName: The Carlsbad Structure and the Minority Attack
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. In the Carlsbad structure White advances the queenside minority (b4–b5) to create a weakness on c6, while Black counters with a central break or play on the kingside.

The structure. White has pawns on a2, b2, d4 and e3. Black has pawns on a7, b7, c6 and d5. White's c-pawn and Black's e-pawn have been exchanged. On the queenside White has two pawns against three, which is why the attack is called a minority attack. The c-file is half-open for White.

The idea. White pushes b2–b4–b5, supported by a2–a4 when needed, to exchange the pawn on c6. After bxc6 bxc6, Black has a weak pawn on c6 and an isolated pawn on a7, and White's rooks aim down the c-file.

M — Move
- Direct threat: has his last move attacked a queenside pawn, or a piece that supports b4?
- Immediate plan: for White, is Black preparing ...c5, ...Ne4 or ...f5? For Black, is White bringing a rook to b1 and preparing b4?
- New weaknesses: which of his pieces left the queenside? Pieces drifting to the kingside leave c6 under-defended.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. The pawn pattern above, the half-open c-file, the squares b5 and c6, and the pieces that defend c6 (a knight on d7, a rook on c8, the queen). Typical White pieces are a bishop on d3, the queen on c2, rooks on b1 and c1. Typical Black pieces are knights on d7 and f6, a bishop on e7 or d6, and a rook on e8.

Alarm Triggers for White — the minority attack is ON when:
- the pawns stand as in the structure above,
- your pieces can support b4 and b5: a rook on b1, the queen on c2 or b3, a knight or bishop eyeing b5 and c6,
- Black has not played ...a5 and has no piece placed to meet b5,
- Black's pieces are committed to the kingside, so c6 is under-defended,
- Black's ...c5 break would not give him an easy game.

Alarm Triggers for Black — the counter-plan is ON when:
- White's rooks are not yet on b1 and c1, so you can break first with ...c5,
- the trade ...Ne4 is available and kingside play with ...f5 is safe,
- ...a5 stops b4 without leaving a fatal weakness,
- a knight can reach c4 after White has committed to b4.

Counter-Alarms. For Black: White's rooks stand on b1 and c1, the pawn is on a4 or b4, Bd3 and Qc2 are ready, and c6 is defended only once. For White: Black's pieces aim at d4 and e3, ...c5 is ready, or ...Ne4 and ...f5 point at your king.

P — Priorities
1. Captures: be ready for bxc6 bxc6 with a rook on the c-file, and for the exchange on b5 if Black takes.
2. Attacks: b4–b5 attacks c6 and is the heart of White's plan. For Black, ...c5 or the knight trade ...Ne4 attacks White's structure.
3. Quiet moves: Rab1, Qc2 or Qb3, a2–a3 and b2–b4 for White; ...Nd7, ...Re8 and ...Nf8 for Black, with the kingside play in mind.
Checks seldom matter here. The structure is a long-term plan, so use the three-second scan first to make sure nothing tactical is hanging.

C — Calculation
- Count the defenders of c6 against the attackers after b5.
- Calculate the exchange b5 cxb5 Bxb5 (or Nxb5): does the c-file now favour White, or does Black get ...c4 or a counter?
- After b5, Black's options (...cxb5, ...c5 or ...a6) each change the structure. Calculate which one leaves him a weakness before you commit.
- Compare the minority attack with the central break e3–e4: at this moment, which plan is faster?
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- White pushes b4–b5 before the rooks and queen are ready.
- White lets Black play ...c5 for free and ends up with nothing.
- White ignores Black's kingside play.
- Black defends c6 passively with no counterplay.
- Black allows b4–b5 without a plan.

Opening Bridge
The Carlsbad is the reference exchange structure for every Queen's Gambit family, so keep it in mind even when your repertoire route avoids it. [B-Slav] It can arise when White exchanges on d5 and Black recaptures with the e-pawn. The Exchange Slav recaptures with the c-pawn instead, which leads to a symmetrical structure with an open c-file (chapter 1.4). Check the repertoire PGN trees for any branch that reaches Carlsbad pawns and tag those positions ch_t2_02.

chapters.chapterName: The Isolated Queen's Pawn (Both Sides)
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. The owner of the isolated queen's pawn (IQP) attacks while the pieces are still on the board; the opponent blockades the square in front of the pawn and trades pieces toward an endgame.

The structure. An IQP is a d-pawn with no c- or e-pawn of its own colour beside it: d4 for White or d5 for Black. A pawn on d4 guards c5 and e5, and the files beside it are open.

Strengths of the pawn. Space, control of c5 and e5, open files for the rooks, a knight outpost on e5, and attacking chances against the kingside, including the d4–d5 break.

Weaknesses of the pawn. It needs protection from pieces. The square in front of it (d5 for White's IQP) is a permanent outpost for the opponent's pieces. In an endgame the pawn is a target.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move attack the isolated pawn, or threaten to occupy the blockade square?
- Immediate plan: for the owner, is he preparing d4–d5 or a kingside attack? For the blockader, is he heading for trades?
- New weaknesses: which piece left the defence of the pawn or the blockade square? Which trade just made the blockade easier?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. The IQP and the blockade square, the open c- and e-files, the activity of both sides' pieces, the bishops, and whether the d4–d5 break works tactically.

Alarm Triggers for the IQP owner — attack is ON when:
- queens and minor pieces are still on the board,
- your pieces can reach the kingside: a bishop on d3, the queen on c2, a knight on e5 or a rook lift,
- the d4–d5 break wins material or opens lines,
- his pieces are not placed to blockade.

Alarm Triggers for the blockader — the blockade plan is ON when:
- a knight can reach d5 (d4 against a Black IQP) and stand there firmly,
- minor pieces and queens can be traded,
- the d4–d5 break is not available to the owner,
- the position is heading toward an endgame.

Counter-Alarms. For the owner: trades are coming and the blockade is in place, so attack now or accept a worse endgame. For the blockader: the owner has pieces massed against your king and the d4–d5 break is one move away.

P — Priorities
Owner. 1. Checks and attacks on the king. 2. Captures that keep the pieces on rather than trading them. 3. The d4–d5 break, only when it wins something concrete.
Blockader. 1. Captures that trade pieces, starting with the owner's active ones. 2. Occupy the blockade square with a knight. 3. Attack the isolated pawn with rooks and the queen once the pieces are coordinated.

C — Calculation
- Owner: count attackers against defenders in the king zone, and check the tactics on d5 and h7 before you push or sacrifice.
- Blockader: check that each trade leaves your own king safe, and calculate which endgame the trades lead to.
- Both: if the isolated pawn moves, count the exchanges on d5 or d4 step by step.
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- The owner trades pieces and drifts into a worse endgame.
- The blockader allows d4–d5 for free.
- The owner attacks with too few pieces.
- The blockader trades pieces and leaves the king exposed to a kingside attack.

Opening Bridge
[B-CK] The Panov-Botvinnik with 5...e6 often leads to IQP positions: after the exchange on d5 and ...Nxd5, White's d4 pawn is isolated. In your repertoire you are on the blockading side. Put a knight on d5, trade pieces, and aim for an endgame in which the isolated pawn is weak. The structure is close to Semi-Slav and Queen's Gambit structures, which is why this line was chosen. [B-Slav] You can meet IQP positions from the other side if a Semi-Slav line leaves a pawn isolated; check the PGN trees for such branches.

chapters.chapterName: Hanging Pawns
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. The owner of hanging pawns keeps the pieces active and advances a pawn only when it wins something concrete; the opponent pressures the pawns and tries to force an advance at the wrong moment.

The structure. Hanging pawns are two adjacent pawns, usually on the c- and d-files, with no friendly pawn on the neighbouring b- and e-files: c4 and d4 for White, c5 and d5 for Black. Together they control four squares (for White: b5, c5, d5 and e5), and the b- and e-files beside them are half-open.

Strengths. Central space, mobility (either pawn may advance), control of key squares and open files for the rooks. The break d4–d5 or c4–c5 can open the game suddenly.

Weaknesses. No pawn defends them, so they need piece support. If one is blocked or attacked and must advance at the wrong moment, or if a trade leaves them without support, they fall. In an endgame they are often weak.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move attack one of the pawns or take away a square that supports them?
- Immediate plan: is he preparing to force an advance, or to blockade the squares in front?
- New weaknesses: which supporting piece has left, and which square is now uncovered?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. The two pawns, the b- and e-files, the squares in front of the pawns, the activity of the pieces, and who owns the bishops.

Alarm Triggers for the owner — the dynamic plan is ON when:
- your pieces are active and aimed at the centre or at his king,
- one pawn can advance with a concrete gain: a piece attacked, a file opened or a passed pawn created,
- his pieces are tied to the squares in front of the pawns.

Alarm Triggers for the opponent — the pressure plan is ON when:
- one pawn, usually the c-pawn on a half-open file, can be attacked by two pieces,
- advancing either pawn would leave the other one weak,
- queens and rooks can be traded, which reduces the owner's attacking chances,
- your pieces control the squares in front of the pawns.

Counter-Alarms. For the owner: the pawns are attacked more often than they are defended, pieces are being traded, or your supporting piece is about to leave. For the opponent: an advance of the pawns would attack a piece, or his rooks are active on the open files.

P — Priorities
Owner. 1. Checks and attacks that use the active pieces. 2. Captures that keep the supporting pieces on the board. 3. The advance, only with a concrete point.
Opponent. 1. Captures that remove supporting pieces. 2. Attacks on the weaker pawn. 3. Quiet moves that control the squares in front of the pawns.

C — Calculation
- Count attackers and defenders of each pawn after every exchange.
- Before an advance, list which pieces and files it opens for both sides.
- Check the endgame that the trades lead to: do the pawns survive?
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- The owner pushes a pawn with no concrete gain.
- The owner trades pieces and leaves the pawns without support.
- The opponent attacks the pawns with only one piece.
- The opponent ignores the advance when it becomes tactically possible.

Opening Bridge
Hanging pawns are not a core structure of the three repertoires, but they appear through transpositions and in your opponents' choices, and players at 1200–1600 meet them often. In Semi-Slav move orders, check the PGN trees for branches that leave the c- and d-pawns side by side, and tag those positions ch_t2_04.

chapters.chapterName: Weak Squares, Outposts and Backward Pawns
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Find the squares and pawns that he can no longer protect with pawns, bring your pieces to them, and guard your own weaknesses the same way.

Key terms.
- Weak square (hole): a square that none of a side's pawns can ever guard again, usually because the neighbouring pawns have advanced.
- Outpost: a weak square in his half of the board, occupied by your piece and supported by one of your pawns. A knight on the fifth or sixth rank is the classic occupant.
- Backward pawn: a pawn behind its neighbours that no pawn can guard and that cannot advance safely, because an enemy pawn controls the square in front of it. It usually stands on a half-open file.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move attack my backward pawn or head for one of my holes?
- Immediate plan: is he rerouting a knight toward an outpost?
- New weaknesses: which pawn move did he just make that can never be reversed? Every such move leaves a square behind it.

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Holes on the third to sixth ranks, pawns that cannot move forward, half-open files, the minor pieces that guard the weak squares, and the routes your knights can take to reach them.

Alarm Triggers — attack the weakness when:
- he pushed a pawn that can never go back (...f6, ...g6, ...h6, ...b6) and left a square behind it,
- a pawn exchange left him with a backward pawn on a half-open file,
- the bishop that guarded that colour of squares has been traded,
- one of your knights can reach the hole in two or three moves,
- you can double rooks on the file in front of a backward pawn.

Counter-Alarms — your own weakness is in danger when:
- you are about to push a pawn that can never be reversed,
- the last minor piece that guards one of your holes is about to be traded,
- his knight is heading for a square that your pawns cannot attack.

P — Priorities
Attacker. 1. Captures: trade the piece that guards the weakness, or capture the backward pawn when it falls. 2. Attacks: put a knight on the outpost and pile rooks on the file. 3. Quiet moves: reroute a piece toward the hole.
Defender. 1. Cover the square with a piece. 2. Trade the attacking knight. 3. Advance the backward pawn with a break.

C — Calculation
- Can the outpost piece be driven away by a pawn move or removed by a trade?
- Count the tempi your piece needs to reach the square against his counterplay.
- Can the weak pawn advance safely, and does that solve his problem?
- What structure do you give up when you trade the guard of the weak square?
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- Pushing a pawn for no reason and creating a hole.
- Putting a knight on an outpost that a pawn can challenge.
- Attacking a backward pawn with only one piece.
- Leaving your own holes unguarded.

Opening Bridge
[W-Colle] The square e5 is the natural outpost for a White knight, supported by the d4 pawn. Black's ...f6 would challenge it but weakens e6 and the light squares. [B-CK] In the Advance structure, White's pawn on e5 takes d6 and f6 away from Black's pieces, so Black should challenge the chain (chapter 2.7) before White's pieces settle on d6.

chapters.chapterName: Piece Exchanges: Which Pieces to Trade
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Trade the pieces that serve your plan, keep the ones that do the work, and before each trade ask what the position looks like after the last recapture.

In Tier 0 you learned when to trade. Here you learn which pieces to trade. The same trade can help you or hurt you, depending on the piece that leaves the board.

M — Move
- Direct threat: is his trade offer also a threat, such as a capture that forks or a recapture that wins a pawn?
- Immediate plan: which of my pieces is he trying to remove, and why? He usually wants a defender of a key square or my best bishop.
- New weaknesses: what changes in my pawn structure, my king cover and my colour complexes if I accept?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. Your best and worst piece, his best and worst piece, the guards of key squares and of his king, the pawn structure after the trade, and the minor-piece balance after the trade.

The Trade Test. Ask five questions before every trade.
1. Worst for best: does the trade remove my worst piece or his best one?
2. Key defender: does it remove a defender of a key square, a weak pawn or his king?
3. Structure: which pawns change? Does he get doubled or isolated pawns, or do I?
4. Imbalance: what is left? The bishop pair, a good bishop against a bad one, opposite-coloured bishops, a knight against a bad bishop?
5. Direction: which endgame does this lead to, and does it suit me?

Alarm Triggers — trade when:
- you are cramped and a trade frees a piece,
- he is attacking and you can trade his most dangerous piece, usually the queen or an attacking bishop,
- the trade removes the defender of a weak pawn or key square,
- your piece is bad and his counterpart is good,
- you are ahead and the trade simplifies the position,
- the trade damages his pawn structure.

Counter-Alarms — keep the pieces when:
- you have space and he is cramped, because trades free him,
- you are attacking and need the pieces,
- the trade would give him the bishop pair in an open position,
- the trade would leave you with a weakness that his remaining piece can attack.

P — Priorities
1. Captures: if a trade leads to a structure you want, make it.
2. Attacks: attack the piece you want to trade, so that he must exchange or move it.
3. Quiet moves: improve your position first, then offer the trade at the best moment.

C — Calculation
- Play the full exchange sequence, including his in-between moves.
- Judge the end position with the five questions of the Trade Test.
- Check whether the recapture can be made with a better piece or a better pawn.
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- Trading to relieve tension without a purpose.
- Trading the wrong bishop.
- Handing him the bishop pair in an open position.
- Trading into an endgame that favours him.
- Ignoring how the recapture changes the pawn structure.

Opening Bridge
[B-CK] In the Classical Caro-Kann the usual bishop trade on d3 removes Black's problem piece, but check the PGN for the exact line. In the Panov, Black's trades are minor pieces and queens against the isolated pawn (chapter 2.3). [W-Colle] White keeps the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 for the attack on h7, so he trades Black's defenders (the knight on f6, a bishop on e7) rather than his own attackers.

chapters.chapterName: Pawn Chains: The Advance Structure and Attacking the Base
chapters.theoryExplanation:
The plan in one sentence. Attack the base of an enemy pawn chain, because when the base falls the whole chain falls; defend your own chain by supporting its base and by playing on the flank where the chain points.

The structure. A pawn chain is a diagonal line of pawns that protect each other, such as White's pawns on d4 and e5. The head is the front pawn (e5) and the base is the rearmost pawn (d4). The chain fixes its pawns on one colour of squares, so the bishop of that colour behind the chain is hemmed in. The chain also takes squares away from the opponent: White's pawn on e5 controls d6 and f6.

Where each side plays. A chain points toward the flank where its owner has space. White's d4–e5 chain points at the kingside, so White expands there, often with f2–f4. The opponent strikes at the base from the other side, with ...c5 and pieces aimed at d4.

M — Move
- Direct threat: does his move attack the base, or prepare a flank break such as f2–f4?
- Immediate plan: is he supporting the base with c3 and Nf3, or preparing to release the tension with dxc5?
- New weaknesses: which piece or pawn left the defence of the base? Has b2 become loose to a queen on b6?

S — Specifics & Alarm Triggers
Board features. The base and the head of the chain, the support of the base (pawns and pieces), the lever against the base (...c5 against d4), the bishop behind the chain, and the flank where the chain points.

Alarm Triggers for the attacker of the base — attack is ON when:
- the base is defended only by pieces, or the supporting pawn on c3 has not been played,
- you can attack the base with a pawn lever (...c5) and add pieces (...Nc6, ...Qb6),
- the owner's pieces are not placed to defend the base,
- your bad bishop can be developed outside the chain.

Alarm Triggers for the owner — defence is ON when:
- you can support the base with c3 and with pieces such as Nf3 and a bishop on e3,
- the chain points at a flank where you can attack, with f2–f4–f5 or Ng5,
- the opponent's lever is not yet supported by pieces.

Counter-Alarms. For the owner: the lever is supported by ...Nc6 and ...Qb6, and your pieces cannot reach d4. For the attacker: the owner's flank break is coming and your bad bishop is still shut in behind the chain.

P — Priorities
Attacker. 1. Captures: ...cxd4 removes the base when it gains something concrete. 2. Attacks: add pressure with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. 3. Quiet moves: free the bad bishop.
Owner. 1. Maintain the base with c3 and piece support. 2. Attack on the flank where the chain points. 3. Decide whether to keep the tension or release it with dxc5.

C — Calculation
- Count attackers and defenders on the base.
- Play out each exchange on d4 and check what a queen on b6 attacks afterwards.
- Check whether the owner's flank break is faster than your attack on the base.
- Run the Two-Question Blunder Check.

Common mistakes
- Attacking only the head of the chain with pieces.
- Leaving the bad bishop locked in behind the chain.
- Letting the owner expand on the flank without counterplay.
- Releasing the tension without a reason.

Opening Bridge
[B-CK] The Advance Variation (1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5) gives White exactly this chain. The line chosen for the Black repertoire, 3...c5, attacks the base from move three. Whether White keeps the tension, takes on c5 or supports d4, the middlegame follows this chapter: keep pressing d4 with pieces and the c-pawn. If White releases the chain with dxc5, the structure opens and chapters 1.5 and 2.5 take over. Check each branch in the PGN and tag its final position.

chapters.chapterName: Minor-Piece Imbalances: Good Knight vs Bad Bishop, the Bishop Pair
